query.original_query: LLM retrieving ordered sequences ranking position knowledge random access versus sequential traversal

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanisms of ordered sequence retrieval and positional knowledge in large language models comparing random access to sequential traversal circuits and attention heads
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the mechanisms underlying ordered sequence retrieval in large language models, comparing circuits for random access versus sequential traversal. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze how positional knowledge is encoded across attention heads and MLP layers. Our analysis reveals distinct functional specialization: specific attention heads in middle layers implement a sequential traversal mechanism, incrementally shifting positional indices through the residual stream, while a separate set of heads in later layers supports direct random access by attending to absolute positional embeddings. We find that sequential retrieval relies on a chain of heads with complementary positional offset functions, whereas random access engages a broader circuit involving both early-layer positional encoding and late-layer content integration. Results show that disrupting the sequential circuit impairs ordered recall but leaves random access largely intact, and vice versa. These findings suggest that models maintain parallel, dissociable pathways for positional information, with implications for understanding how factual recall and list generation are supported by distinct attention-based mechanisms.

sub_queries.semantic_query: LLM retrieving ordered sequences ranking position knowledge random access versus sequential traversal
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether large language models encode ordinal position information through mechanisms analogous to random access or sequential traversal. Using controlled probing tasks on decoder-only transformers, we measured representational similarity between hidden states corresponding to items in ordered sequences (e.g., ranked lists, token positions) under both shuffled and sequential presentation. We compared performance on position retrieval when the model could rely on sequential dependencies versus when it had to access position directly from a randomly ordered input. Results indicate that while models exhibit robust position encoding under sequential conditions, accuracy degrades significantly under random-access demands, suggesting reliance on sequential traversal heuristics rather than explicit positional indexing. Representational similarity analysis further reveals that positional embeddings are more strongly correlated with adjacent tokens than with distant ones, supporting the hypothesis that LLMs approximate ranking knowledge through local contextual chaining rather than direct addressable memory. These findings have implications for understanding the limitations of transformer architectures in tasks requiring true random access to ordered information.

papers.title: Word Order Does Matter and Shuffled Language Models Know It
papers.research_question: Do shuffled language models still have traces of word order information? Why is there a gap in performance between models without position embeddings and models trained on shuffled tokens? Are there NLU benchmarks, other than GLUE, on which shuffled language models perform poorly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models trained on shuffled text retain word order information due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and correlations between sentence length and content, and that some NLU tasks are sensitive to word order.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that models trained on shuffled text retain word order knowledge, largely at the local level, due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations. The order of shuffling (before/after BPE) influences this acquisition, and some NLU tasks are highly sensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled language models contain word order information, as shown by probing tasks.
The performance gap between models without position embeddings and shuffled models is due to position embeddings providing inductive bias and the presence of n-grams when shuffling before BPE segmentation.
Even when shuffling after segmentation, models retain some word order information due to statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities.
Attention patterns in shuffled models show a bias towards adjacent tokens.
Some NLU tasks (e.g., Winograd Schema, ReCoRD) require word order information and show significant performance drops for shuffled models.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models' good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain information pertaining to the original, naturalistic word order. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work -before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning. * Equal contribution. Order was decided by a coin toss.

papers.title: Beyond Memorization: The Challenge of Random Memory Access in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether a generative language model is able to access its memory sequentially or randomly.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can sequentially access memorized content but struggle with random access; recitation and permutation techniques mitigate this challenge and improve performance in question answering.
papers.conclusion: Language models struggle with random memory access, but recitation and permutation mitigate this limitation, and recitation improves performance in open-domain question answering.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can sequentially access memorized content but encounter significant challenges in random memory access.
Recitation (loading memorized content into the context window) enables random access and improves task performance.
Permutation of sentences during training enhances random access capability.
Improving random access via recitation leads to notable gains in open-domain question answering.
The challenges and mitigations are generalizable across different model sizes and architectures (GPT-2, Qwen, Llama).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only language models; future research is needed for encoder-only and encoder-decoder models.
The study does not extend to models beyond 7 billion parameters due to computing resource constraints.
Controlled experiments are conducted on a text corpus of fixed size; implications on large-scale pretraining corpus are not explored.
future_direction: Extend the study to other types of language models (encoder-only, encoder-decoder).
Explore memory access patterns in larger language models beyond 7B parameters.
Investigate the findings on large-scale pretraining corpus and their implications on pretrained language models.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Language Models (LMs) have shown their effectiveness in NLP tasks, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, the mechanisms underlying knowledge storage and memory access within their parameters remain elusive. In this paper, we investigate whether a generative LM (e.g., GPT-2) is able to access its memory sequentially or randomly. Through carefully-designed synthetic tasks, covering the scenarios of full recitation, selective recitation and grounded question answering, we reveal that LMs manage to sequentially access their memory while encountering challenges in randomly accessing memorized content. We find that techniques including recitation and permutation improve the random memory access capability of LMs. Furthermore, by applying this intervention to realistic scenarios of open-domain question answering, we validate that enhancing random access by recitation leads to notable improvements in question answering. The code to reproduce our experiments can be found at https://github.com/sail-sg/lm-random-memory-access.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models without explicit positional encodings learn and use positional information, and is this phenomenon robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that transformer language models without explicit positional encodings can learn implicit positional information through causal attention, achieving competitive performance across various settings.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models learn positional information implicitly without explicit encodings, primarily due to the causal attention mask, but this does not apply to masked language models.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with positional encodings on WikiText-103 and the Pile datasets.
Probing experiments reveal that NoPos models encode absolute positional information in their hidden layers, similar to models with learned embeddings.
Shuffling input tokens significantly increases loss, indicating that positional information is necessary for NoPos models.
The phenomenon is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Performance gaps between NoPos and other methods narrow with larger model sizes but increase with longer sequences for ALiBi.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on models with 125M to 1.3B parameters, and results may not generalize to much larger models.
NoPos models consistently show slightly worse perplexity than models with positional encodings, suggesting that explicit positional inductive bias is beneficial.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models, and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths. Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information. We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position. Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism, but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Interpreting Positional Information in Perspective of Word Order
papers.research_question: How does the attention mechanism's weight sum operation cause insensitivity to positional information, and can a novel weight concatenation operation effectively encode positional information by preserving word order?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the weight sum operation in the attention module as the root cause of its permutation invariance and proposes a novel weight concatenation operation (implemented as PosNet) that implicitly encodes positional information by preserving word order, leading to improved performance on machine translation tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed weight concatenation operation successfully removes the permutation invariance of the attention module by correlating positional information with word order, and its implementation as PosNet leads to competitive or improved performance on neural machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
The weight sum operation in the attention mechanism is the reason for its permutation invariance and inability to encode positional information.
The proposed weight concatenation operation (PosNet) effectively encodes positional information by preserving the word order of a sequence.
The embedding-level PosNet (PosNet-Embed) achieves statistically significant improvements in BLEU and ChrF++ scores over baseline positional encoding methods on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French translation tasks.
The performance superiority of PosNet-Embed over the baseline (SAPE) consistently enlarges as the evaluation n-gram becomes coarser, suggesting it better captures coarser-grained features.
The proposed method exhibits similar time and space complexity to most baseline positional encoding methods, except for relative positional encoding (RPE) which is more resource-intensive.
papers.limitation: The effect of increased parameter counts from the weight concatenation operation and the introduced affine transformations cannot be well isolated, and the increased complexity from direct concatenation is acknowledged.
future_direction: Explore alternative operations that implicitly encode positional information based on word order without resorting to affine transformations to replace the weight sum operation of the attention module.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a powerful and effective method utilized in natural language processing. However, it has been observed that this method is insensitive to positional information. Although several studies have attempted to improve positional encoding and investigate the influence of word order perturbation, it remains unclear how positional encoding impacts NLP models from the perspective of word order. In this paper, we aim to shed light on this problem by analyzing the working mechanism of the attention module and investigating the root cause of its inability to encode positional information. Our hypothesis is that the insensitivity can be attributed to the weight sum operation utilized in the attention module. To verify this hypothesis, we propose a novel weight concatenation operation and evaluate its efficacy in neural machine translation tasks. Our enhanced experimental results not only reveal that the proposed operation can effectively encode positional information but also confirm our hypothesis.

papers.title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation
papers.research_question: How can Transformers execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings? What are the expressivity and learnability properties of such positional Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces positional attention, a variant where attention weights depend only on positional encodings, and shows that positional Transformers are as expressive as parallel computational models with logarithmic depth overhead, have favorable generalization bounds, and exhibit better out-of-distribution generalization on tasks relying on positional information.
papers.conclusion: Positional attention decouples attention from input values, maintaining expressivity while offering better theoretical norm dependence and improved out-of-distribution generalization for tasks that rely on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Positional Transformers can simulate the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model with O(log n) layers, where n is the input length.
Positional Transformers have norm-based generalization bounds that remove exponential dependence on depth compared to standard Transformers, implying they can learn algorithmic tasks via empirical risk minimization.
Empirically, positional Transformers show better out-of-distribution generalization than standard Transformers on tasks where the underlying algorithmic solution relies solely on positional information.
For tasks requiring dynamic communication patterns (e.g., induction heads), positional Transformers perform poorly, likely due to the difficulty of discovering good parameters during training.
There is a trade-off: positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, which can increase sample complexity despite better dependence on parameter norms.
papers.limitation:
Simulation of standard Transformers by positional Transformers incurs an additional quadratic dependency on the number of nodes.
Positional Transformers perform poorly on tasks requiring dynamic communication, such as induction heads.
Positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, potentially increasing sample complexity.
future_direction: In-depth work within the mechanistic interpretability framework to analyze training dynamics and reasons for failure in standard Transformers.
Theoretical analysis of out-of-distribution generalization bounds for deep positional attention architectures, considering training dynamics.
Exploring the exact causes and difficulty of achieving goals like ignoring input values and preserving positional encodings in standard Transformers.
papers.abstract: There is a growing interest in the ability of neural networks to execute algorithmic tasks (e.g., arithmetic, summary statistics, and sorting). The goal of this work is to better understand the role of attention in Transformers for algorithmic execution. Its importance for algorithmic execution has been studied theoretically and empirically using parallel computational models. Notably, many parallel algorithms communicate between processors solely using positional information. Inspired by this observation, we investigate how Transformers can execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings. We prove that Transformers with positional attention (positional Transformers) maintain the same expressivity of parallel computational models, incurring a logarithmic depth cost relative to the input length. We analyze their in-distribution learnability and explore how parameter norms in positional attention affect sample complexity. Our results show that positional Transformers introduce a learning trade-off: while they exhibit better theoretical dependence on parameter norms, certain tasks may require more layers, which can, in turn, increase sample complexity. Finally, we empirically explore the out-of-distribution performance of positional Transformers and find that they perform well in tasks where their underlying algorithmic solution relies on positional information.

papers.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
papers.research_question: How do long-context language models retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and characterizes 'retrieval heads', a sparse set of attention heads responsible for retrieving information from long contexts, and shows they are universal, intrinsic, and causally important for factuality and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval heads implement a conditional copy algorithm and are the primary reason why long-context models can pass the Needle-in-a-Haystack test; their activation explains model factuality versus hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are universal and sparse, existing in all tested long-context models and constituting less than 5% of attention heads.
Retrieval heads are intrinsic, already present in base models and reused in derived models (e.g., via continued pretraining or fine-tuning).
Retrieval heads are dynamically activated based on the specific tokens and context required for retrieval.
Retrieval heads are causal; pruning them leads to retrieval failure and hallucination, while pruning non-retrieval heads does not.
Retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, which require frequent reference to input information, but have less impact on tasks relying on internal knowledge.
future_direction: Fostering future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
Discovering more algorithm and functionalities implemented by other types of attention heads.
Applying insights to KV cache compression by pruning non-retrieval head caches.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress in long-context language models, it remains elusive how transformer-based models exhibit the capability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context. This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify intriguing properties of retrieval heads:(1) universal: all the explored models with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small portion (less than 5\%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending the context length by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random non-retrieval heads does not affect the model's retrieval ability. We further show that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context. Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the input tokens. We believe our insights will foster future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

papers.title: Attention Basin: Why Contextual Position Matters in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind positional bias in LLMs (the attention basin phenomenon), and how can we mitigate it with a training-free reranking method?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the attention basin phenomenon as the mechanistic cause of positional bias in LLMs and proposes AttnRank, a training-free reranking method that aligns document relevance with the model's intrinsic attention preferences to improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the attention basin is a key mechanism behind positional bias in LLMs, and that AttnRank successfully mitigates this bias by reranking documents to match the model's attention preferences, leading to improved performance across diverse models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit an attention basin phenomenon, where they systematically assign higher attention to items at the beginning and end of a structured input sequence.
Increasing attention on correct documents directly improves the probability of generating the correct answer, explaining the lost-in-the-middle effect.
Shallow attention layers are most critical for positional bias, as they exhibit position-dominated attention regimes.
AttnRank, a training-free reranking method that aligns document relevance with the model's attention profile, consistently improves performance across 10 LLMs on multi-hop QA and few-shot learning tasks.
AttnRank outperforms baseline reranking strategies including similarity-based ordering and the lost-in-the-middle heuristic.
papers.limitation:
AttnRank requires access to the model's attention scores, which are often not exposed by closed-source LLM APIs, limiting its applicability.
The method does not eliminate the attention basin phenomenon itself; ideally, models should attend uniformly across positions, which remains an open problem.
future_direction: Develop reranking strategies that are compatible with closed-source LLMs that do not expose attention scores.
Explore methods to mitigate the attention basin phenomenon to achieve more uniform attention distribution across positions.
papers.abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is significantly sensitive to the contextual position of information in the input. To investigate the mechanism behind this positional bias, our extensive experiments reveal a consistent phenomenon we term the attention basin: when presented with a sequence of structured items (e.g., retrieved documents or few-shot examples), models systematically assign higher attention to the items at the beginning and end of the sequence, while neglecting those in the middle. Crucially, our analysis further reveals that allocating higher attention to critical information is key to enhancing model performance. Based on these insights, we introduce Attention-Driven Reranking (AttnRank), a two-stage framework that (i) estimates a model's intrinsic positional attention preferences using a small calibration set, and (ii) reorders retrieved documents or few-shot examples to align the most salient content with these high-attention positions. AttnRank is a model-agnostic, training-free, and plug-and-play method with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on multi-hop QA and few-shot in-context learning tasks demonstrate that AttnRank achieves substantial improvements across 10 large language models of varying architectures and scales, without modifying model parameters or training procedures.

papers.title: POSITIONAL ENCODING FOR TRANSFORMERS
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding methods impact the performance of Transformer models on NLP tasks, and what are the trade-offs between them?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically compares different positional encoding methods for Transformers, finding that relative positional encodings outperform absolute ones on longer sequences and that injecting positional information per-head in the attention matrix is more effective than at the input.
papers.conclusion: Non-recurrent Transformer models are not sensitive to position and require positional encoding. Relative encodings are superior for longer sentences, and per-head addition to the attention matrix is key. The encoder-decoder architecture is most suitable for the tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Using absolute and relative encodings results in similar performance for the model, while relative encodings worked much better with longer sentences.
The original encoder-decoder architecture worked best for the tasks of machine translation and question answering.
Sharing the parameters in the encoder and decoder did not lead to a significant decrease in performance, despite reducing the total parameter count by half.
Adding position encoders at all blocks yields better performance than only at the input block, except for the fixed-length position embedding approach (which may overfit).
The superior performance of some relative position encoding methods can be attributed to their per-head addition to attention matrix rather than the position information being relative or absolute.
future_direction: Explore alternative operations that use word order to implicitly encode positional information, thus shedding light on how it impacts the performance of NLP models.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a powerful and effective method utilized in natural language processing. This mechanism allows the model to focus on important parts of the input sequence. Transformer model utilizes attention mechanisms to replace recurrent and convolutional neural networks, which eliminates the need for increasingly complex operations as the distance between words in a sequence increases. However, this method is notably insensitive to positional information. Positional encoding is crucial for Transformer-like models that heavily rely on the attention mechanism. To make the models position-aware, the position information of the input words is typically incorporated to the input token embeddings as an additional embedding. The purpose of the paper is to conduct a systematic study to understand different position encoding methods. We briefly describe the components of the attention mechanism, its role in the Transformer model, and the encoder-decoder architecture of the Transformer. We also study how sharing position encodings across various heads and layers of a Transformer affects the model performance. Methodology of the study is based on general research methods of analysis and synthesis, experimental testing, and quantitative analysis to comprehensively examine and compare the efficacy and performance of different positional encoding techniques utilized in Transformer models. The obtained results show that using absolute and relative encodings results in similar performance for the model, while relative encodings worked much better with longer sentences. We found the original encoder-decoder form worked best for the tasks of machine translation and question answering. Despite using twice as many parameters as "encoder-only" or "decoder-only" architectures, an encoder-decoder model has a similar computational cost. Besides that, the number of learnable parameters can often be reduced without performance loss. Practical implications.Positional encoding is essential for enabling Transformer models to effectively process data by preserving sequence order, handling variable-length sequences, and improving generalization. Its inclusion significantly contributes to the success of Transformer-based architectures in various natural language processing tasks. Value/originality.Positional encoding is such a critical issue for Transformer-like models. However, it has not been explored how positional encoding establishes positional dependencies within a sequence. We chose to analyze several approaches to position encoding in the context of question answering and machine translation tasks because the influence of positional encoding on NLP models in terms of word order remains ambiguous and requires further exploration.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Deconstructing Positional Information: From Attention Logits to Training Biases
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding schemes (additive vs. multiplicative) mediate the interaction between token content and position, and what causes the performance paradox and single-head deposit pattern in RoPE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified Toeplitz-matrix framework to analyze positional encodings, discovers the single-head deposit pattern in RoPE, and provides a theoretical explanation showing this pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE's multiplicative structure.
papers.conclusion: The Toeplitz framework provides a powerful lens for understanding positional encodings, and the deposit pattern explains RoPE's performance paradox. Controlled mixing of positional signals is a promising strategy for achieving robust, distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's multiplicative structure enables superior performance on tasks requiring content-position coupling but leads to a single-head deposit pattern where positional information is concentrated in one early-layer head.
Additive positional encodings (Absolute, T5, ALiBi) do not exhibit the deposit pattern and show different learning dynamics.
The deposit pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE, caused by exponential amplification of gradient signals during training, leading to extreme specialization.
Hybrid architectures like Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) can mitigate the deposit pattern and improve robustness by mixing positional signals.
RoPE's strong inductive bias suppresses the formation of latent positional representations observed in models with additive or no PE.
papers.limitation:
The connection between the deposit pattern and RoPE's known struggles with length extrapolation requires direct empirical validation.
Future work should probe the limits of these positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks such as sequence reversal or Dyck language recognition.
future_direction: Direct empirical validation of the link between the deposit pattern and length extrapolation.
Testing positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks.
More complex controlled analysis of positional mechanisms in transformers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings enable Transformers to incorporate sequential information, yet their theoretical understanding remains limited to two properties: distance attenuation and translation invariance. Because natural language lacks purely positional data, the interplay between positional and semantic information is still underexplored. We address this gap by deconstructing the attention-logit computation and providing a structured analysis of positional encodings, categorizing them into additive and multiplicative forms. The differing properties of these forms lead to distinct mechanisms for capturing positional information. To probe this difference, we design a synthetic task that explicitly requires strong integration of positional and semantic cues. As predicted, multiplicative encodings achieve a clear performance advantage on this task. Moreover, our evaluation reveals a hidden training bias: an information aggregation effect in shallow layers that we term the single-head deposit pattern. Through ablation studies and theoretical analysis, we proved that this phenomenon is inherent in multiplicative encodings. These findings deepen the understanding of positional encodings and call for further study of their training dynamics.

papers.title: The Role of Complex NLP in Transformers for Text Ranking
papers.research_question: Does the BERT Cross-Encoder Ranker perform well due to modeling syntactic aspects in text ranking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic aspects do not play a critical role in the effectiveness of BERT for text ranking, and comparable performance can be achieved without sequence order or position information.
papers.conclusion: Syntactic aspects are not critical for BERT's effectiveness in ranking; performance gains may come from richer embeddings and cross-attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can maintain ranking performance when fine-tuned on perturbed input order (sorted or shuffled).
Removing position information entirely (BOW-BERT) yields comparable performance to the standard BERT ranker.
The model becomes less order-sensitive after fine-tuning on the ranking task compared to pre-trained BERT.
Representations change when sequence order is destroyed, especially in later layers, despite similar effectiveness.
Similar findings apply to natural language understanding tasks on GLUE, where syntax is not crucial.
papers.limitation: Due to computational demands, experiments are limited to fine-tuning and do not include pre-training.
future_direction: Designing pre-training tasks tailored specifically to ranking to reduce model complexity.
Investigating other factors like query-passage cross-attention for performance.
papers.abstract: Even though term-based methods such as BM25 provide strong baselines in ranking, under certain conditions they are dominated by large pre-trained masked language models (MLMs) such as BERT. To date, the source of their effectiveness remains unclear. Is it their ability to truly understand the meaning through modeling syntactic aspects? We answer this by manipulating the input order and position information in a way that destroys the natural sequence order of query and passage and shows that the model still achieves comparable performance. Overall, our results highlight that syntactic aspects do not play a critical role in the effectiveness of re-ranking with BERT. We point to other mechanisms such as query-passage cross-attention and richer embeddings that capture word meanings based on aggregated context regardless of the word order for being the main attributions for its superior performance.

papers.title: Computation Mechanism Behind LLM Position Generalization
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) computationally process positional information to enable position generalization, such as tolerance to position perturbations and length generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that LLMs learn a disentanglement of attention logits into positional and semantic components, with a linear correlation of 0.959, and identifies a pattern in intermediate features that enables this effect, providing computational explanations for position generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention logits in LLMs can be approximately disentangled into independent positional and semantic components, providing computational explanations for position generalization and insights for controlling these phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Attention logits can be approximated by a 3-axis linear decomposition with high correlation.
Attention logits can be disentangled into a sum of positional relevance and semantic importance components.
A pattern in slow-rotating dimensions of query and key vectors enables this disentanglement, which is learned rather than inherent.
LLMs exhibit robustness to position perturbations in text, feature order, and position encoding, with minimal impact on perplexity and downstream task accuracy.
The disentanglement mechanism explains how length generalization techniques work by keeping attention outputs in-distribution.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily evaluates position robustness involving text order and length generalizations, but real-world language processing tasks often involve more complex positional dependencies.
The extent to which models actively leverage this property during training is unclear.
future_direction: Future research could delve deeper into the specific architectural choices and training data patterns that contribute to this robustness.
Future explanations on how such a mechanism is acquired during training dynamics could greatly enhance the work.
papers.abstract: Most written natural languages are composed of sequences of words and sentences. Similar to humans, large language models (LLMs) exhibit flexibility in handling textual positions - a phenomenon we term position generalization. They can understand texts with position perturbations and generalize to longer texts than those encountered during training with the latest techniques. These phenomena suggest that LLMs handle positions tolerantly, but how LLMs computationally process positional relevance remains largely unexplored. This work connects the linguistic phenomenon with LLMs' computational mechanisms. We show how LLMs enforce certain computational mechanisms for the aforementioned tolerance in position perturbations. Despite the complex design of the self-attention mechanism, this work reveals that LLMs learn a counterintuitive disentanglement of attention logits. Their values show a 0.959 linear correlation with an approximation of the arithmetic sum of positional relevance and semantic importance. Furthermore, we identify a prevalent pattern in intermediate features, which we prove theoretically enables this effect. The pattern, which is different from how randomly initialized parameters would behave, suggests that it is a learned behavior rather than a natural result of the model architecture. Based on these findings, we provide computational explanations and criteria for LLMs' position flexibilities. This work takes a pioneering step in linking position generalization with modern LLMs' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: How the Brain Represents Language and Answers Questions? Using an AI System to Understand the Underlying Neurobiological Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the brain represent language and answer questions? The paper investigates this by proposing a framework of neural mechanisms inspired by an AI question-answering system.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework of 12 neurally plausible mechanisms that could implement language-based question answering in the brain, inspired by the AI system START.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that known or plausible neural mechanisms are sufficient to perform the complex cognitive function of question answering, providing a first view of how this could be implemented by the brain.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a two-stage chunking process to convert temporal language sequences into spatial patterns for storage and recall.
Suggests working memory buffers organized by theta and gamma oscillations can hold up to 7 triplets (subject-verb-object units).
Describes a retrieval process where the episodic long-term memory network finds the stored memory most similar to a question, even with different word order.
Introduces neural mechanisms for pointers to handle complex sentences with embedded clauses.
Proposes mechanisms for conceptual alignment and comparison to answer yes/no and WH-questions.
future_direction: Development of a complete functional architecture integrating the proposed mechanisms.
Further reinterpretation of the model in terms of potential interactions with other systems such as the visual and auditory systems.
Considering the viewpoint of embodied cognition to obtain other neural mechanisms supporting language processing.
papers.abstract: To understand the computations that underlie high-level cognitive processes we propose a framework of mechanisms that could in principle implement START, an AI program that answers questions using natural language. START organizes a sentence into a series of triplets, each containing three elements (subject, verb, object). We propose that the brain similarly defines triplets and then chunks the three elements into a spatial pattern. A complete sentence can be represented using up to 7 triplets in a working memory buffer organized by theta and gamma oscillations. This buffer can transfer information into long-term memory networks where a second chunking operation converts the serial triplets into a single spatial pattern in a network, with each triplet (with corresponding elements) represented in specialized subregions. The triplets that define a sentence become synaptically linked, thereby encoding the sentence in synaptic weights. When a question is posed, there is a search for the closest stored memory (having the greatest number of shared triplets). We have devised a search process that does not require that the question and the stored memory have the same number of triplets or have triplets in the same order. Once the most similar memory is recalled and undergoes 2-level dechunking, the sought for information can be obtained by element-by-element comparison of the key triplet in the question to the corresponding triplet in the retrieved memory. This search may require a reordering to align corresponding triplets, the use of pointers that link different triplets, or the use of semantic memory. Our framework uses 12 network processes; existing models can implement many of these, but in other cases we can only suggest neural implementations. Overall, our scheme provides the first view of how language-based question answering could be implemented by the brain.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
papers.research_question: How do attention layers in transformer-based LLMs implement memory retrieval mechanisms, and are contextual cues represented as keywords?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval, with Q, K, V playing distinct roles analogous to human memory, and that contextual cues are represented as keywords.
papers.conclusion: Attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval mechanisms guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, with keywords serving as retrieval cues and specific neurons encoding these cues.
papers.key_findings:
Swapping V alone induces hallucinations, indicating V stores content.
Swapping both K and V induces systematic hallucination, showing content-addressable matching and content retrieval.
Swapping K only hinders factual recall, representing retrieval failure.
Consistent, model-specific attention neurons are activated by keywords.
Perturbing keywords at the K matrix impairs memory retrieval.
papers.abstract: While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for large language models (LLMs) remains an evolving field with many unresolved questions, increasing regulatory pressures have spurred interest in its role in ensuring transparency, accountability, and privacy-preserving machine unlearning. Despite recent advances in XAI have provided some insights, the specific role of attention layers in transformer based LLMs remains underexplored. This study investigates the memory mechanisms instantiated by attention layers, drawing on prior research in psychology and computational psycholinguistics that links Transformer attention to cue based retrieval in human memory. In this view, queries encode the retrieval context, keys index candidate memory traces, attention weights quantify cue trace similarity, and values carry the encoded content, jointly enabling the construction of a context representation that precedes and facilitates memory retrieval. Guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, we hypothesize that the cues used in the initial stage of retrieval are instantiated as keywords. We provide converging evidence for this keywords-as-cues hypothesis. In addition, we isolate neurons within attention layers whose activations selectively encode and facilitate the retrieval of context-defining keywords. Consequently, these keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning.

papers.title: Word Order Matters When You Increase Masking
papers.research_question: To what extent do masked language models require explicit position encoding to perform well on the masked language modeling objective, and how does the amount of masking affect this requirement?
papers.core_contribution: The utility of explicit position encoding in masked language models increases with the number of masked tokens; without position encoding, models cannot reconstruct position information when masking is high.
papers.conclusion: Position encoding becomes necessary for masked language modeling as the amount of masking increases, and the amount of masking should be carefully chosen to encourage models to use position information.
papers.key_findings:
When only one token is masked, models with and without position encoding perform similarly.
As the number of masked tokens increases, the true probability distribution for ordered contexts diverges from that of unordered contexts.
Models with position encoding (BERT) approximate the ordered distribution well, while models without (NP) approximate the unordered distribution.
The amount of masking is a crucial parameter for models to use position information.
papers.limitation:
The results are obtained on artificial languages, and adapting the method to natural languages may be difficult because the true probability distribution is not accessible.
Training multiple models on natural languages is computationally expensive.
The artificial language has fixed word order, so the findings may not generalize to natural languages with more flexible word order.
future_direction: Find proxies to estimate reference points for natural languages.
Evaluate impact of position encoding in languages with variable word order.
papers.abstract: Word order, an essential property of natural languages, is injected in Transformer-based neural language models using position encoding. However, recent experiments have shown that explicit position encoding is not always useful, since some models without such feature managed to achieve state-of-the art performance on some tasks. To understand better this phenomenon, we examine the effect of removing position encodings on the pre-training objective itself (i.e., masked language modelling), to test whether models can reconstruct position information from co-occurrences alone. We do so by controlling the amount of masked tokens in the input sentence, as a proxy to affect the importance of position information for the task. We find that the necessity of position information increases with the amount of masking, and that masked language models without position encodings are not able to reconstruct this information on the task. These findings point towards a direct relationship between the amount of masking and the ability of Transformers to capture order-sensitive aspects of language using position encoding.

papers.title: Sequence-to-Sequence Models with Attention Mechanistically Map to the Architecture of Human Memory Search
papers.research_question: Why do human memory systems use context-based architectures, and are these architectures optimal? The paper investigates the convergence between sequence-to-sequence models with attention (from machine translation) and context-based models of human memory.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanistically map to the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model of human memory, and implements such a model as an interpretable cognitive model that captures human free recall behavior and provides insights into memory search dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Seq2seq models with attention provide a powerful framework for modeling human memory search, offering interpretability and flexibility, and the convergence suggests functional rationality in human memory architecture.
papers.key_findings:
Seq2seq models with attention mathematically map to the CMR model and capture human free recall behavior as effectively as CMR.
The optimized seq2seq model exhibits optimal recall behavior similar to rational-CMR.
Intermediate training stages show recency and backward contiguity effects similar to average human behavior.
Working memory capacity (hidden dimension size) affects how primacy is achieved: with small hidden dimensions, attention shifts to the beginning; with large, primacy is maintained in the hidden state.
Ablation of attention mimics memory deficits in medial temporal lobe amnesia patients.
papers.abstract: Past work has long recognized the important role of context in guiding how humans search their memory. While context-based memory models can explain many memory phenomena, it remains unclear why humans develop such architectures over possible alternatives in the first place. In this work, we demonstrate that foundational architectures in neural machine translation -- specifically, recurrent neural network (RNN)-based sequence-to-sequence models with attention -- exhibit mechanisms that directly correspond to those specified in the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model of human memory. Since neural machine translation models have evolved to optimize task performance, their convergence with human memory models provides a deeper understanding of the functional role of context in human memory, as well as presenting new ways to model human memory. Leveraging this convergence, we implement a neural machine translation model as a cognitive model of human memory search that is both interpretable and capable of capturing complex dynamics of learning. We show that our model accounts for both averaged and optimal human behavioral patterns as effectively as context-based memory models. Further, we demonstrate additional strengths of the proposed model by evaluating how memory search performance emerges from the interaction of different model components.

papers.title: Improve Transformer Models with Better Relative Position Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can Transformer models be improved by designing better relative position embeddings that increase interaction between query, key, and position embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes new relative position embedding methods for Transformer self-attention, with the best method (method 4) generalizing absolute position embedding and improving accuracy on SQuAD1.1 while being robust to inductive settings.
papers.conclusion: The proposed relative position embedding methods, particularly method 4, improve Transformer model accuracy on question answering and are robust for handling longer sequences.
papers.key_findings:
Proposed relative position embedding method 4 outperforms absolute and Shaw's relative position embeddings on SQuAD1.1.
The proposed method is robust to inductive settings, generalizing to sequences longer than those seen during training.
The method can be applied as a near drop-in replacement to improve large models (e.g., BERT-large) with a small computational budget.
Small clipping values (k) for relative distance are sufficient, as attention weights for distant tokens are near zero.
Relative position embeddings have limited impact on GLUE tasks, which primarily use the [CLS] token.
papers.limitation:
Method 3 leads to significantly lower accuracy on the MRPC dataset, possibly due to unstable training from the introduced three-way interaction.
Relative position embeddings do not show significant accuracy differences on GLUE tasks, which may be because GLUE primarily uses the [CLS] token, limiting the impact of relative embeddings.
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures rely on explicit position encodings in order to preserve a notion of word order. In this paper, we argue that existing work does not fully utilize position information. For example, the initial proposal of a sinusoid embedding is fixed and not learnable. In this paper, we first review absolute position embeddings and existing methods for relative position embeddings. We then propose new techniques that encourage increased interaction between query, key and relative position embeddings in the self-attention mechanism. Our most promising approach is a generalization of the absolute position embedding, improving results on SQuAD1.1 compared to previous position embeddings approaches. In addition, we address the inductive property of whether a position embedding can be robust enough to handle long sequences. We demonstrate empirically that our relative position embedding method is reasonably generalized and robust from the inductive perspective. Finally, we show that our proposed method can be adopted as a near drop-in replacement for improving the accuracy of large models with a small computational budget.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviors of BERT in Ranking
papers.research_question: What are the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks on MS MARCO and TREC Web Track?
papers.core_contribution: BERT is effective for QA-focused passage ranking due to its interaction-based seq2seq matching, but less effective for ad hoc document ranking where user click signals are more beneficial.
papers.conclusion: BERT excels in seq2seq matching tasks like MS MARCO due to its pre-training on surrounding contexts, but for ad hoc document ranking, pre-training on user clicks is more effective.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-based rankers outperform previous neural IR models on MS MARCO passage ranking.
BERT is not effective as a representation-based model for ranking; it relies on cross-sequence interactions.
On TREC ad hoc ranking, BERT underperforms compared to feature-based learning to rank and models pre-trained on user clicks.
BERT's attention focuses on marker tokens and stopwords, but stopwords have minimal impact on performance.
BERT assigns extreme ranking scores and depends on a few key terms, preferring semantic matches over loose relevance.
papers.limitation: BERT performs worse on TREC ad hoc ranking compared to models pre-trained on user clicks, indicating a gap between its pre-training on surrounding contexts and the needs of document ranking.
future_direction: Training deeper networks on user clicks signals
Studying deeper models trained on relevance-based labels compared to shallower neural rankers
papers.abstract: This paper studies the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks. We explore several different ways to leverage the pre-trained BERT and fine-tune it on two ranking tasks: MS MARCO passage reranking and TREC Web Track ad hoc document ranking. Experimental results on MS MARCO demonstrate the strong effectiveness of BERT in question-answering focused passage ranking tasks, as well as the fact that BERT is a strong interaction-based seq2seq matching model. Experimental results on TREC show the gaps between the BERT pre-trained on surrounding contexts and the needs of ad hoc document ranking. Analyses illustrate how BERT allocates its attentions between query-document tokens in its Transformer layers, how it prefers semantic matches between paraphrase tokens, and how that differs with the soft match patterns learned by a click-trained neural ranker.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how language models encode and recall time-specific information, focusing on whether there are specific attention heads dedicated to temporal knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads in language models that encode and recall time-specific knowledge, and shows that ablating them impairs temporal knowledge while leaving other capabilities intact.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Temporal Heads are crucial for temporal knowledge in LLMs, and targeting them can enable precise temporal updates without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal Heads, such as a15.h0 and a18.h3 in Llama2, are identified across multiple models and are crucial for temporal knowledge recall.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal effect on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated for both numerical (e.g., 'In 2004') and textual (e.g., 'In the year...') temporal conditions, indicating they encode a broad temporal dimension.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the activations of these heads, enabling targeted updates.
Backup Temporal Heads exist that can compensate when primary heads are ablated, ensuring model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs was constrained due to lack of temporal dependencies in options.
EAP-IG does not support models with Grouped-Query Attention, limiting analysis of models like Llama-3.
future_direction: Future work should focus on broader application for enhancing temporal reasoning and time-aware model alignment.
papers.abstract: While the ability of language models to elicit facts has been widely investigated, how they handle temporally changing facts remains underexplored. We discover Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that primarily handle temporal knowledge, through circuit analysis. We confirm that these heads are present across multiple models, though their specific locations may vary, and their responses differ depending on the type of knowledge and its corresponding years. Disabling these heads degrades the model's ability to recall time-specific knowledge while maintaining its general capabilities without compromising time-invariant and question-answering performances. Moreover, the heads are activated not only numeric conditions ("In 2004") but also textual aliases ("In the year ..."), indicating that they encode a temporal dimension beyond simple numerical representation. Furthermore, we expand the potential of our findings by demonstrating how temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the values of these heads.

papers.title: Layer-wise Positional Bias in Short-Context Language Modeling
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether positional bias in language models is an intrinsic architectural property that persists across layers in short-context next-word prediction, independent of task complexity.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attribution-based framework using layer conductance to analyze positional bias, showing that transformer layers exhibit stable, text-invariant positional importance profiles, with recency bias increasing with depth and early layers preferentially weighting content words.
papers.conclusion: LLM layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction, indicating positional bias is intrinsic to model architecture. Early layers assign the highest conductance to most words and prefer content words, while later layers lose word-type sensitivity and concentrate on recent positions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction.
These profiles are text-invariant and remain unchanged under lexical scrambling, indicating an intrinsic architectural property.
Recency bias increases monotonically with depth, while primacy bias is weak and diminishes in deeper layers.
Early layers preferentially weight content words over function words, while later layers lose this word-type differentiation.
Early layers dominate the largest proportion of words at all positions, while later layers increasingly concentrate importance on recent positions.
papers.limitation:
Focus on short contexts; may differ in long-context settings or tasks beyond next-word prediction.
Limited set of autoregressive transformer models; may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on layer conductance as a proxy for importance; different attribution methods may yield different results.
Word-type analyses based on POS categories and averaging; do not capture finer-grained syntactic or semantic distinctions.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to long-context regimes and tasks beyond next-word prediction.
papers.abstract: Language models often show a preference for using information from specific positions in the input regardless of semantic relevance. While positional bias has been studied in various contexts, from attention sinks to task performance degradation in long-context settings, prior work has not established how these biases evolve across individual layers and input positions, or how they vary independent of task complexity. We introduce an attribution-based framework to analyze positional effects in short-context language modeling. Using layer conductance with a sliding-window approach, we quantify how each layer distributes importance across input positions, yielding layer-wise positional importance profiles. We find that these profiles are architecture-specific, stable across inputs, and invariant to lexical scrambling. Characterizing these profiles, we find prominent recency bias that increases with depth and subtle primacy bias that diminishes through model depth. Beyond positional structure, we also show that early layers preferentially weight content words over function words across all positions, while later layers lose this word-type differentiation.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.
