Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: RankSteer: Activation Steering for Pointwise LLM Ranking
papers.research_question: Do LLMs internally encode separable directions for role, relevance, and decision-making, and can these directions be isolated and manipulated to steer ranking behavior?
papers.core_contribution: We propose RankSteer, a post-hoc activation steering framework for zero-shot pointwise LLM ranking that disentangles and jointly controls decision, evidence, and role directions in the representation space, improving ranking performance without modifying model weights or explicitly introducing cross-document comparisons.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering provides an efficient post-hoc calibration mechanism for pointwise LLM rankers, recovering under-utilized ranking capacity with far fewer labeled queries than fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
RankSteer improves ranking performance on TREC DL 2020 and BEIR benchmarks using only a small set of anchor queries.
RankSteer is competitive with pairwise, setwise, and listwise methods while maintaining the efficiency of pointwise ranking.
Activation steering recovers under-utilized ranking capacity more effectively than fine-tuning when supervision is scarce.
Steering reduces dispersion in the ranking geometry, making the ranking structure more stable.
The method is robust to the number of anchor queries, with even a single anchor query yielding competitive performance.
future_direction: The development of activation steering methods for other ranking paradigms and retrieval settings should be investigated.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong performance as zero-shot rankers, yet their effectiveness is highly sensitive to prompt formulation, particularly role-play instructions. Prior analyses suggest that role-related signals are encoded along activation channels that are largely separate from query-document representations, raising the possibility of steering ranking behavior directly at the activation level rather than through brittle prompt engineering. In this work, we propose RankSteer, a post-hoc activation steering framework for zero-shot pointwise LLM ranking. We characterize ranking behavior through three disentangled and steerable directions in representation space: a \textbf{decision direction} that maps hidden states to relevance scores, an \textbf{evidence direction} that captures relevance signals not directly exploited by the decision head, and a \textbf{role direction} that modulates model behavior without injecting relevance information. Using projection-based interventions at inference time, RankSteer jointly controls these directions to calibrate ranking behavior without modifying model weights or introducing explicit cross-document comparisons. Experiments on TREC DL 20 and multiple BEIR benchmarks show that RankSteer consistently improves ranking quality using only a small number of anchor queries, demonstrating that substantial ranking capacity remains under-utilized in pointwise LLM rankers. We further provide a geometric analysis revealing that steering improves ranking by stabilizing ranking geometry and reducing dispersion, offering new insight into how LLMs internally represent and calibrate relevance judgments.

papers.title: Some Attention is All You Need for Retrieval
papers.research_question: Does training in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures lead to overlapping capabilities or strict functional segregation, particularly for retrieval tasks?
papers.core_contribution: We demonstrate complete functional segregation in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures: retrieval depends exclusively on self-attention layers. Sparsifying attention to just 15% of heads maintains near-perfect retrieval while preserving 84% MMLU performance, suggesting self-attention specializes primarily for retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: We established complete functional segregation in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures: retrieval depends exclusively on self-attention layers while SSMs handle general language capabilities. This functional segregation enables immediate practical optimizations such as targeted sparsification, specialized retrieval modules, and component-specific deployment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention ablation causes catastrophic retrieval failure (0% accuracy) across RecurrentGemma-2B/9B and Jamba-Mini-1.6, while SSM layers show no compensatory mechanisms even with improved prompting.
Sparsifying attention to just 15% of heads maintains near-perfect retrieval and preserves 84% MMLU performance, indicating that self-attention specializes primarily for retrieval.
Successful retrieval requires needle token exposure during generation and sufficient contextual information during prefill or generation phases.
The effect of prefill sparsification reduces with increasing model size, as seen in Jamba versus RecurrentGemma models.
The Binary manipulation (uniform attention weights) fails, indicating that precise attention weight patterns are necessary for retrieval.
papers.limitation:
The entropy-based sparsification method is suboptimal, as indicated by the sparsified configuration performing worse than the ablated configuration on GLUE.
The Binary manipulation method was not thoroughly investigated before employment, and the method used to unify and binarize attention weights may have been inadequate.
future_direction: Compare state transition matrices between pure and hybrid SSM variants to uncover how retrieval mechanisms differ when attention is available versus absent.
Structurally investigate attention heads through an offline analysis that examines the weights of different circuits in the self-attention architecture, as performed by Olsson et al. (2022).
Explore whether the functional specialization emerges from architectural constraints or training dynamics, and whether lightweight retrieval-specific mechanisms could replace full attention layers.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate complete functional segregation in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures: retrieval depends exclusively on self-attention layers. Across RecurrentGemma-2B/9B and Jamba-Mini-1.6, attention ablation causes catastrophic retrieval failure (0% accuracy), while SSM layers show no compensatory mechanisms even with improved prompting. Conversely, sparsifying attention to just 15% of heads maintains near-perfect retrieval while preserving 84% MMLU performance, suggesting self-attention specializes primarily for retrieval tasks. We identify precise mechanistic requirements for retrieval: needle tokens must be exposed during generation and sufficient context must be available during prefill or generation. This strict functional specialization challenges assumptions about redundancy in hybrid architectures and suggests these models operate as specialized modules rather than integrated systems, with immediate implications for architecture optimization and interpretability.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Randomized Positional Encodings Boost Length Generalization of Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do Transformers fail to generalize to sequences of arbitrary length, and how can randomized positional encodings overcome this?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces randomized positional encodings that allow Transformers to generalize to sequences of unseen length by preventing out-of-distribution positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: Randomized positional encodings significantly improve length generalization in Transformers while maintaining efficiency, offering a promising approach for handling longer sequences.
papers.key_findings:
Randomized positional encodings increase test accuracy by 12.0% on average on algorithmic reasoning tasks.
The method is 35.4 times faster than training on longer sequences due to quadratic attention complexity.
Randomized encodings prevent out-of-distribution activations for longer sequences.
Sorting the subsampled positions is crucial for performance.
The method works with various positional encoding schemes like sin/cos, relative, ALiBi, RoPE, and learned.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is confined to synthetic algorithmic reasoning tasks, not natural language.
Introduces a new hyperparameter L, the maximum sequence position.
Only addresses one failure mode of length generalization; other factors exist.
future_direction: Evaluation on SCAN, CFQ, COGS, or the Long Range Arena to assess generalizability.
Further research on other factors contributing to poor length generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformers have impressive generalization capabilities on tasks with a fixed context length. However, they fail to generalize to sequences of arbitrary length, even for seemingly simple tasks such as duplicating a string. Moreover, simply training on longer sequences is inefficient due to the quadratic computation complexity of the global attention mechanism. In this work, we demonstrate that this failure mode is linked to positional encodings being out-of-distribution for longer sequences (even for relative encodings) and introduce a novel family of positional encodings that can overcome this problem. Concretely, our randomized positional encoding scheme simulates the positions of longer sequences and randomly selects an ordered subset to fit the sequence's length. Our large-scale empirical evaluation of 6000 models across 15 algorithmic reasoning tasks shows that our method allows Transformers to generalize to sequences of unseen length (increasing test accuracy by 12.0% on average).

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: How Reliable are LLMs for Reasoning on the Re-ranking task?
papers.research_question: How do different training methods affect the semantic understanding of LLMs for re-ranking tasks, and can LLMs generate informed textual reasoning for re-ranking decisions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable re-ranking method that combines LLM training with SHAP-based token attribution and natural language explanation generation, finding DPO to be the most effective training method and that explanations with attribution scores are more coherent.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of generating logical and interpretable explanations for re-ranked items using LLMs and SHAP, with DPO identified as the most effective training method for re-ranking.
papers.key_findings:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) consistently achieves the lowest loss and highest accuracy across all evaluated LLMs for the re-ranking task.
Large Language Models (especially Qwen 7B) significantly outperform the classical BM25 baseline in re-ranking effectiveness.
Explanations generated with token attribution scores (from SHAP) are more coherent and relevant than those generated without such scores.
The proposed method can generate logical and interpretable explanations for re-ranked items, enhancing transparency.
future_direction: Conduct both qualitative and quantitative analyses of explanation quality across a wide range of re-ranking use cases, incorporating human evaluations and automated explainability metrics.
papers.abstract: With the improving semantic understanding capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), they exhibit a greater awareness and alignment with human values, but this comes at the cost of transparency. Although promising results are achieved via experimental analysis, an in-depth understanding of the LLM's internal workings is unavoidable to comprehend the reasoning behind the re-ranking, which provides end users with an explanation that enables them to make an informed decision. Moreover, in newly developed systems with limited user engagement and insufficient ranking data, accurately re-ranking content remains a significant challenge. While various training methods affect the training of LLMs and generate inference, our analysis has found that some training methods exhibit better explainability than others, implying that an accurate semantic understanding has not been learned through all training methods; instead, abstract knowledge has been gained to optimize evaluation, which raises questions about the true reliability of LLMs. Therefore, in this work, we analyze how different training methods affect the semantic understanding of the re-ranking task in LLMs and investigate whether these models can generate more informed textual reasoning to overcome the challenges of transparency or LLMs and limited training data. To analyze the LLMs for re-ranking tasks, we utilize a relatively small ranking dataset from the environment and the Earth science domain to re-rank retrieved content. Furthermore, we also analyze the explainable information to see if the re-ranking can be reasoned using explainability.

papers.title: Rotary Offset Features in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are rotary offset features in large language models and how do they influence attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of rotary offset features in LLMs with rotary positional embeddings and derives bounds that predict their occurrence and properties.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals consistent patterns of rotary offset features across model architectures and scales, and the derived bounds can help improve understanding, context length extension, and quantization for models using rotary embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Rotary offset features (large-magnitude features in rotary feature pairs) exist consistently across layers, heads, and model architectures.
These features are found at low rotary frequencies that do not complete a full period within the context length.
An upper bound on the rotary frequency predicts which frequencies give rise to rotary offset features.
A lower bound predicts the minimum angle between query-key pairs for rotary offset features.
Rotary offset features influence attention patterns, including the selection of attention sinks.
future_direction: Altering the distribution of rotary frequencies to make LLMs adopt context length extension more effectively.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on positional encodings to provide sequence position information to their attention mechanism. Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE), which encode relative position by rotating queries and keys, have become widely used in modern LLMs. We study the features and patterns that emerge in queries and keys when using rotary embeddings and introduce the concept of rotary offset features. Our analysis reveals that these features, which frequently exhibit large activations and are often interpreted as outliers, arise consistently across layers, attention heads, and model architectures. We derive bounds predicting which rotary frequencies give rise to rotary offset features and the minimum angle between the query-key pairs for these features. We verify our predictions empirically across models of different sizes and architectures.

papers.title: On Scalar Embedding of Relative Positions in Attention Models
papers.research_question: Why does scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) work well in attention models, and how can it be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, and proposes AT5, a new SRPE method with a learnable bucketing function and constrained bucket embeddings, which outperforms T5 on several tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's SRPE, identifies its limitations, and proposes the AT5 model which improves upon T5 and may apply to other NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SRPE in attention can be interpreted as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, with the final attentive distribution being the posterior given the input sequence.
T5's SRPE has two weaknesses: a fixed heuristic bucketing function and independent bucket embeddings, which can lead to underfitting and overfitting respectively.
The proposed AT5 model, with a learnable bucketing function and MLP-constrained embeddings, achieves superior performance to T5 on artificial tasks, text classification, question answering, and machine translation.
Quantitative analysis shows AT5 learns more meaningful prior probability distributions over relative positions compared to T5.
Ablation studies indicate that higher-probability heads in AT5 contribute more to its performance gain compared to T5.
papers.abstract: Attention with positional encoding has been demonstrated as a powerful component in modern neural network models, such as transformers. However, why positional encoding works well in attention models remains largely unanswered. In this paper, we study the scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) proposed in the T5 transformer. Such an encoding method has two features. First, it uses a scalar to embed relative positions. Second, the relative positions are bucketized using a fixed heuristic algorithm, and positions in the same bucket share the same embedding. In this work, we show that SRPE in attention has an elegant probabilistic interpretation. More specifically, the positional encoding serves to produce a prior distribution for the attended positions. The resulting attentive distribution can be viewed as a posterior distribution of the attended position given the observed input sequence. Furthermore, we propose a new SRPE (AT5) that adopts a learnable bucketization protocol and automatically adapts to the dependency range specific to the learning task. Empirical studies show that the AT5 achieves superior performance than the T5's SRPE.

papers.title: Mechanism Shift During Post-training from Autoregressive to Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: Does post-training autoregressive models into masked diffusion models induce genuine bidirectional reasoning mechanisms, or do they merely repackage autoregressive heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Post-training autoregressive models into masked diffusion models induces a task-dependent mechanism shift, preserving autoregressive circuitry for local causal tasks but rewiring for global planning tasks with increased early-layer processing and distributed semantic integration.
papers.conclusion: Masked diffusion post-training induces a task-dependent mechanism shift, preserving autoregressive mechanisms for local causal reasoning while reorganizing them for more globally integrated, non-sequential reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
For the local causal task (IOI), MDMs largely preserve the autoregressive circuitry inherited from their ARM initializations.
For the global reasoning task (Countdown), MDMs show low circuit overlap with ARMs and a strong shift in computation to earlier layers (lower Center of Gravity).
MDMs transition from sharp, localized component specialization (as in ARMs) to distributed semantic integration across components.
At the neuron level, early layers in MDMs exhibit reduced task-specific selectivity and more uniform activation profiles compared to ARMs.
Diffusion post-training reorganizes internal computation rather than merely adjusting parameters, supporting non-sequential global planning.
papers.limitation:
The study is confined to two benchmark tasks (IOI and Countdown), limiting generalizability.
The circuits identified are task-specific findings rather than universal signatures of autoregressive or masked diffusion models.
The attribution-guided pipeline does not constitute an exhaustive characterization of all computations underlying model behavior.
papers.abstract: Post-training pretrained Autoregressive models (ARMs) into Masked Diffusion models (MDMs) has emerged as a cost-effective strategy to overcome the limitations of sequential generation. However, the internal algorithmic transformations induced by this paradigm shift remain unexplored, leaving it unclear whether post-trained MDMs acquire genuine bidirectional reasoning capabilities or merely repackage autoregressive heuristics. In this work, we address this question by conducting a comparative circuit analysis of ARMs and their MDM counterparts. Our analysis reveals a systematic "mechanism shift" dependent on the structural nature of the task. Structurally, we observe a distinct divergence: while MDMs largely retain autoregressive circuitry for tasks dominated by local causal dependencies, they abandon initialized pathways for global planning tasks, exhibiting distinct rewiring characterized by increased early-layer processing. Semantically, we identify a transition from sharp, localized specialization in ARMs to distributed integration in MDMs. Through these findings, we conclude that diffusion post-training does not merely adapt model parameters but fundamentally reorganizes internal computation to support non-sequential global planning.

papers.title: CoPE: A Lightweight Complex Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to enhance positional encoding in transformers by leveraging complex-valued encoding to separately capture semantic content and positional information.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoPE, a lightweight complex positional encoding that uses phase-aware attention to separate semantic and positional information, avoids long-term decay, is compatible with linear attention, and achieves superior performance on GLUE benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CoPE is a novel positional encoding that encodes context and position through real and imaginary components, demonstrating effectiveness in capturing positional dependencies with computational efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
CoPE does not exhibit long-term decay in attention scores.
CoPE is compatible with linear attention mechanisms.
CoPE achieves lower training loss and better test performance on some GLUE datasets compared to RoPE, Sinusoidal, and Learned encodings.
CoPE has lower computational complexity than RoPE.
Phase-aware attention in the first layer effectively captures positional dependencies.
papers.limitation:
Extrapolation: sinusoidal embeddings may underperform when extrapolated beyond trained sequence length.
Evaluation is limited to smaller models trained from scratch due to resource constraints, not on pretraining or fine-tuning tasks with larger models.
future_direction: Extrapolation experiments with CoPE
Evaluation on pretraining and fine-tuning tasks with larger models
Applications to diverse sequence modeling tasks
papers.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of position encoding in transformer architectures. By incorporating positional information, this approach provides essential guidance for modeling dependencies between elements across different sequence positions. We introduce CoPE (a lightweight Complex Positional Encoding), a novel architecture that leverages complex-valued encoding to encode both content and positional information. Our approach replaces traditional positional encodings with complex embeddings where the real part captures semantic content and the imaginary part encodes positional information. We introduce phase-aware attention in the first layer of the transformer model to capture position-dependent patterns, followed by standard attention layers for higher-levels. We show that CoPE doesn't exhibit long term decay and is compatible with linear attention. Experimental evaluation on the GLUE benchmark suggest that our approach achieves superior performance with less computational complexity, compared to RoPE, Sinusoidal and Learned positional encodings.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Neurons in Large Language Models: Dead, N-gram, Positional
papers.research_question: What are the roles and properties of FFN neurons in large language models, specifically regarding dead neurons, n-gram detectors, and positional neurons, and how do they change with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that FFN neurons in large language models exhibit sparsity (dead neurons), act as token and n-gram detectors that explicitly suppress their triggering tokens, and encode positional information, with these properties changing with model scale.
papers.conclusion: FFN neurons in LLMs play diverse roles including dead neurons, n-gram detectors that suppress their triggers, and positional neurons, indicating that the key-value memory view of FFNs is incomplete and their roles are still poorly understood.
papers.key_findings:
Many FFN neurons are 'dead' (never activate) especially in early layers, and larger models are more sparse.
Alive neurons in early layers often act as token and n-gram detectors, with each neuron dedicated to a small set of tokens or n-grams.
Token-detecting neurons not only promote next token candidates but also suppress the triggering tokens, indicating explicit removal of current token information from the residual stream.
Some neurons are positional, activating based on token position regardless of textual content, and they often collaborate to cover position ranges.
With scale, models have more dead neurons and token detectors, and encode position less explicitly (moving away from absolute position).
papers.limitation:
Dead neurons might correspond to patterns so rare that they are not encountered in the data used.
The 350m model behaves differently due to implementation details (LayerNorm placement), showing that modeling choices affect interpretability.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms that remove information from the residual stream further.
Further understand the roles of FFN layers beyond the key-value memory view.
papers.abstract: We analyze a family of large language models in such a lightweight manner that can be done on a single GPU. Specifically, we focus on the OPT family of models ranging from 125m to 66b parameters and rely only on whether an FFN neuron is activated or not. First, we find that the early part of the network is sparse and represents many discrete features. Here, many neurons (more than 70% in some layers of the 66b model) are "dead", i.e. they never activate on a large collection of diverse data. At the same time, many of the alive neurons are reserved for discrete features and act as token and n-gram detectors. Interestingly, their corresponding FFN updates not only promote next token candidates as could be expected, but also explicitly focus on removing the information about triggering them tokens, i.e., current input. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of mechanisms specialized at removing (rather than adding) information from the residual stream. With scale, models become more sparse in a sense that they have more dead neurons and token detectors. Finally, some neurons are positional: them being activated or not depends largely (or solely) on position and less so (or not at all) on textual data. We find that smaller models have sets of neurons acting as position range indicators while larger models operate in a less explicit manner.

papers.title: Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and are these properties due to architectural biases or learned from training data?
papers.core_contribution: Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and these properties are likely learned from the statistical patterns in training data rather than being inherent to the transformer architecture.
papers.conclusion: The human-like memory properties observed in Large Language Models are likely learned from statistical patterns in human-generated text, suggesting that human memory characteristics influence the structure of narratives.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit primacy and recency effects in memory recall.
Adding elaborations to facts improves recall accuracy.
Forgetting in LLMs occurs primarily through interference rather than memory decay.
Repetitions improve recall, with spaced repetitions being more effective than immediate ones.
LLMs show a 'memory formation time' where recall improves with initial distance from the presented facts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are huge artificial neural networks which primarily serve to generate text, but also provide a very sophisticated probabilistic model of language use. Since generating a semantically consistent text requires a form of effective memory, we investigate the memory properties of LLMs and find surprising similarities with key characteristics of human memory. We argue that the human-like memory properties of the Large Language Model do not follow automatically from the LLM architecture but are rather learned from the statistics of the training textual data. These results strongly suggest that the biological features of human memory leave an imprint on the way that we structure our textual narratives.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: A Universal Emergent Decomposition of Retrieval Tasks in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models internally solve retrieval tasks? Is there a universal modular decomposition across models and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers a universal emergent modular decomposition of retrieval tasks in language models' layers and demonstrates a proof-of-concept application for scalable internal oversight to mitigate prompt injection.
papers.conclusion: The study presents evidence of an emergent decomposition of retrieval tasks across models and tasks, and shows that interpretability can be turned into practical solutions for scalable internal oversight of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Language models decompose retrieval tasks modularly: middle layers at the last token position process the request, while late layers retrieve the correct entity from the context.
Request-patching (residual stream patching at middle layers) allows modular combination of request and context from different inputs, preserving over 70% of the original correct token probability in most model-task pairs.
This decomposition is universal across 18 models (125M to 70B parameters) and six task domains (e.g., question answering, translation, coding).
Fine-grained analysis on Pythia-2.8b shows request processing is distributed across attention heads and MLPs, while retrieval is more localized.
The decomposition enables a proof-of-concept internal oversight method that mitigates prompt injection, improving accuracy from 15.5% to 97.5% on Pythia-12b with human supervision on only a single input.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to retrieval tasks with a simple structure.
The application is a proof of concept limited to a single simple question-answering task.
future_direction: Extending the ORION input structure to include more advanced requests (e.g., more filtering conditions).
Automating dataset creation using frontier LMs like GPT-4 to generate large sets of tasks from problem specifications.
Applying dataset design principles to other types of tasks beyond retrieval.
papers.abstract: When solving challenging problems, language models (LMs) are able to identify relevant information from long and complicated contexts. To study how LMs solve retrieval tasks in diverse situations, we introduce ORION, a collection of structured retrieval tasks spanning six domains, from text understanding to coding. Each task in ORION can be represented abstractly by a request (e.g. a question) that retrieves an attribute (e.g. the character name) from a context (e.g. a story). We apply causal analysis on 18 open-source language models with sizes ranging from 125 million to 70 billion parameters. We find that LMs internally decompose retrieval tasks in a modular way: middle layers at the last token position process the request, while late layers retrieve the correct entity from the context. After causally enforcing this decomposition, models are still able to solve the original task, preserving 70% of the original correct token probability in 98 of the 106 studied model-task pairs. We connect our macroscopic decomposition with a microscopic description by performing a fine-grained case study of a question-answering task on Pythia-2.8b. Building on our high-level understanding, we demonstrate a proof of concept application for scalable internal oversight of LMs to mitigate prompt-injection while requiring human supervision on only a single input. Our solution improves accuracy drastically (from 15.5% to 97.5% on Pythia-12b). This work presents evidence of a universal emergent modular processing of tasks across varied domains and models and is a pioneering effort in applying interpretability for scalable internal oversight of LMs.

papers.title: Understanding the Skill Gap in Recurrent Language Models: The Role of the Gather-and-Aggregate Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can the Transformer-SSM performance gap be traced to algorithmic capabilities in a few specific heads?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the Gather-and-Aggregate mechanism as a key bottleneck in in-context retrieval, explaining the performance gap between Transformers and SSMs, and shows that hybrid models can mitigate this gap by delegating aggregation to attention layers.
papers.conclusion: The Transformer-SSM performance gap is largely due to differences in a small number of retrieval-critical heads implementing the Gather-and-Aggregate mechanism, and hybrid models can effectively merge the strengths of both architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Both Transformer and SSM models rely on a few specialized heads for in-context retrieval, implementing a Gather-and-Aggregate mechanism.
Disabling a single Gather or Aggregate head in a pruned Llama-3.1-8B model drastically reduces MMLU accuracy from 66% to 25%.
SSMs exhibit smoother attention patterns, making sharp token transitions difficult and requiring more heads for effective retrieval.
Hybrid models delegate Aggregate Head functionality to attention layers, and replacing a single G&A head in an SSM with attention improves retrieval performance.
The retrieval bottleneck can obscure limited knowledge demands, as models can succeed on MMLU with functioning G&A heads but fail on other knowledge benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The G&A interaction does not always occur in consecutive layers, and pruning-based methods may not always identify interacting layers.
future_direction: Determining optimal placement and refining architectural choices for hybrid models.
Exploring hybrid designs that merge strengths of Transformers and SSMs.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to Transformers for long sequences, but their fixed-size recurrent state limits capability on algorithmic tasks, such as retrieving past context. In this work, we examine how in-context retrieval operates in Transformer- and SSM-based language models and find that both rely on a similar Gather-and-Aggregate (G&A) mechanism: a Gather Head extracts relevant information pieces from context, which an Aggregate Head integrates into a single representation. In both architectures, G&A concentrates in a few heads, forming critical bottlenecks even for simple retrieval. For example, we show that disabling a single Gather or Aggregate Head in a pruned Llama-3.1-8B impairs retrieving the correct answer letter in MMLU, reducing its accuracy from 66% to 25% (random guessing). Moreover, this retrieval bottleneck can obscure limited knowledge demands of tasks as the pruned model succeeds on MMLU with functioning G&A heads yet fails on other knowledge benchmarks. The bottleneck similarly extends to tasks where SSMs typically underperform, such as GSM8K, BBH, and dialogue comprehension. We show that SSMs' retrieval challenges manifest in these heads, creating smoother attention patterns instead of the sharp token transitions effective G&A requires. Thus, the Transformer-SSM retrieval gap exists in just a few heads, rather than the entire language model. This suggests a unified explanation for Transformer vs. SSM performance gap while showing how to merge their strengths. We find that pretrained hybrid models, where SSMs are combined with a few attention layers, delegate the role of Aggregate Heads to attention. Similarly, replacing a single G&A head in a pretrained SSM with an attention variant boosts retrieval and benchmark scores.

papers.title: Latent Positional Information is in the Self-Attention Variance of Transformer Language Models Without Positional Embeddings
papers.research_question: Where is positional information stored in transformer language models without positional embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without positional embeddings inherently encode strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance, an effect that persists after pre-training.
papers.conclusion: Positional information is encoded in the self-attention variance of transformer language models without positional embeddings, justifying their removal for more efficient pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
The variance of the self-attention output in a randomly initialized transformer language model without positional embeddings decreases as the token position increases, providing latent positional information.
This variance shrinkage effect is attributed to the interaction between the causal attention mask and the transformer architecture.
The derived variance properties for the randomly initialized model are also observed in the lower layers of a fully pre-trained model.
BERT without positional embeddings fails to encode positional information because its bidirectional attention leads to constant variance across all positions.
Predicting the position of later tokens is more challenging due to the plateauing of variance for larger positions.
papers.limitation: The analysis relies on assumptions of a randomly initialized and frozen TLM and randomly sampled input tokens, which do not hold for human languages and pre-trained TLMs.
future_direction: Analyze the training dynamics of a TLM to understand the model parameter distribution after pre-training.
Use Zipf's law or n-gram language models to quantify the degree of input token duplication in human languages for a more accurate variance estimate.
papers.abstract: The use of positional embeddings in transformer language models is widely accepted. However, recent research has called into question the necessity of such embeddings. We further extend this inquiry by demonstrating that a randomly initialized and frozen transformer language model, devoid of positional embeddings, inherently encodes strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance. To quantify this variance, we derive the underlying distribution of each step within a transformer layer. Through empirical validation using a fully pretrained model, we show that the variance shrinkage effect still persists after extensive gradient updates. Our findings serve to justify the decision to discard positional embeddings and thus facilitate more efficient pretraining of transformer language models.

papers.title: Interpreting Context Look-ups in Transformers: Investigating Attention-MLP Interactions
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly, providing a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads process context and use next-token neurons to help predict a word associated with, but not previously seen in that context, providing insight into how attention heads can work with MLP neurons to predict new words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can recognize contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron.
An automated method can explain and characterize interactions between attention heads and token-predicting neurons.
The head explanation score can be used to evaluate the quality of explanations.
The phenomenon is observed across different model families and sizes (GPT-2 and Pythia variants).
Ablation experiments confirm that the identified attention heads are causally involved in predicting the token.
papers.limitation:
Focus on max-activating behavior of neurons, which might overlook subtler activation patterns.
Reliance on a maximum of 30 prompts per neuron.
GPT-4 struggles with longer prompts and may generate poor explanations for certain patterns (like induction-style prompts).
Scope limited to neurons whose associated tokens are whole words and prompts shorter than 100 tokens.
future_direction: Investigate whether this phenomenon happens to such neurons throughout their range of activations.
Look into whether multiple attention heads could work with a single next-token neuron.
Look into whether a single attention head could work with multiple next-token neurons.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for advancing their theoretical foundations and real-world applications. While the attention mechanism and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have been studied independently, their interactions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words. We propose a methodology to identify next-token neurons, find prompts that highly activate them, and determine the upstream attention heads responsible. We then generate and evaluate explanations for the activity of these attention heads in an automated manner. Our findings reveal that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly. This mechanism provides a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction. Our approach offers a foundation for further research into the intricate workings of LLMs and their impact on text generation and understanding.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Optimal ablation for interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we better quantify the importance of model components for interpretability by using an ablation method that minimizes expected loss?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces optimal ablation (OA), a method for ablating model components by setting them to a constant that minimizes expected loss, leading to better component importance estimates and improved performance in circuit discovery, factual recall localization, and latent prediction.
papers.conclusion: Optimal ablation is a theoretically and empirically better method for ablating model components, improving component importance quantification and downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OA provides a theoretically grounded way to measure component importance by minimizing spoofing effects.
OA yields lower ablation loss gaps compared to prior methods like zero, mean, resample, and counterfactual ablation.
OA improves circuit discovery, producing smaller and lower-loss circuits.
OA improves causal tracing for factual recall, providing more precise localization.
OA improves latent prediction via OCA lens, achieving better predictive power and causal faithfulness.
papers.limitation: OA requires optimizing constants for each component and subtask, which can be computationally expensive.
future_direction: More efficient optimization methods for OA constants
Scaling interpretability techniques to larger models
papers.abstract: Interpretability studies often involve tracing the flow of information through machine learning models to identify specific model components that perform relevant computations for tasks of interest.
