Equipping Transformers with index-based addressing mechanisms could enable them to learn algorithmic tasks more generally.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers fail at length generalization in algorithmic tasks like parity and addition due to their inability to perform random memory access (index-based addressing).
Using an interleaved scratchpad format that places the current active bit and running parity adjacent eliminates the need for random access and enables perfect length generalization.
Adding mnemonics (random tokens) to the scratchpad allows Transformers to perform random access indirectly via content-based addressing, enabling length generalization.
Attention map visualizations show that without mnemonics, the model fails to attend to the correct bit beyond the training length, while with mnemonics, the attention pattern is near-perfect.
The effectiveness of mnemonics depends on their alignment between input and output and their randomness; constant or non-aligned mnemonics do not work.
future_direction: Equipping Transformers with effective index-based addressing mechanisms to enable learning of algorithmic tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite their recent successes, Transformer-based large language models show surprising failure modes. A well-known example of such failure modes is their inability to length-generalize: solving problem instances at inference time that are longer than those seen during training. In this work, we further explore the root cause of this failure by performing a detailed analysis of model behaviors on the simple parity task. Our analysis suggests that length generalization failures are intricately related to a model's inability to perform random memory accesses within its context window. We present supporting evidence for this hypothesis by demonstrating the effectiveness of methodologies that circumvent the need for indexing or that enable random token access indirectly, through content-based addressing. We further show where and how the failure to perform random memory access manifests through attention map visualizations.

papers.title: Theoretical Limitations of Self-Attention in Neural Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical computational capabilities of self-attention to model formal languages, specifically hierarchical structures and periodic finite-state languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that self-attention cannot model periodic finite-state languages (like PARITY) or hierarchical structure (like DYCK) unless the number of layers or heads increases with input length.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention has limited computational power and cannot model periodic regular languages or basic recursion, which theoretically confirms that it is more restricted than recurrent architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers with hard attention cannot recognize the regular language PARITY or the context-free language DYCK.
For soft attention, transformers cannot achieve perfect cross-entropy when modeling distributions over these formal languages.
The limitations hold unless the number of layers or heads grows with the input length.
The results are asymptotic and may not apply to short input sequences.
Self-attention cannot emulate stacks or general finite-state automata, unlike recurrent networks.
papers.limitation: The results are asymptotic, showing mistakes on sufficiently long inputs, but a transformer may perform well on short inputs by using large numbers of layers and heads.
future_direction: Complementing the asymptotic methods with empirical studies or non-asymptotic extensions.
Investigating connections between sensitivity of functions and generalization in feedforward networks.
papers.abstract: Transformers are emerging as the new workhorse of NLP, showing great success across tasks. Unlike LSTMs, transformers process input sequences entirely through self-attention. Previous work has suggested that the computational capabilities of self-attention to process hierarchical structures are limited. In this work, we mathematically investigate the computational power of self-attention to model formal languages. Across both soft and hard attention, we show strong theoretical limitations of the computational abilities of self-attention, finding that it cannot model periodic finite-state languages, nor hierarchical structure, unless the number of layers or heads increases with input length. These limitations seem surprising given the practical success of self-attention and the prominent role assigned to hierarchical structure in linguistics, suggesting that natural language can be approximated well with models that are too weak for the formal languages typically assumed in theoretical linguistics.

papers.title: Eliminating Position Bias of Language Models: A Mechanistic Approach
papers.research_question: How can position bias in language models be eliminated without training, using a mechanistic approach?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PINE, a training-free method that eliminates position bias in language models by making inter-document attention bidirectional and re-assigning document positions based on attention-derived importance scores.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel train-free zero-shot approach to eliminate position bias mechanically by making every input document equally affected by attention mask and position embedding.
papers.key_findings:
Position bias in language models is caused by causal attention and position embedding.
PINE eliminates position bias and improves model performance on LM-as-a-judge, retrieval-augmented QA, molecule generation, and math reasoning tasks.
PINE is particularly effective for reasoning tasks, enabling Llama-3-70B-Instruct to outperform GPT-4 models on the RewardBench reasoning set.
PINE outperforms baseline methods such as PCW and Structured Prompting.
PINE incurs acceptable computational overhead (2x to 8x wall time) and memory cost.
papers.limitation: PINE requires extra computation overhead (2x to 8x wall time compared to vanilla inference).
future_direction: Improving the efficiency of PINE with more efficient implementation.
papers.abstract: Position bias has proven to be a prevalent issue of modern language models (LMs), where the models prioritize content based on its position within the given context. This bias often leads to unexpected model failures and hurts performance, robustness, and reliability across various applications. Our mechanistic analysis attributes the position bias to two components employed in nearly all state-of-the-art LMs: causal attention and relative positional encodings. Based on the analyses, we propose to eliminate position bias (e.g., different retrieved documents' orders in QA affect performance) with a training-free zero-shot approach. Our method changes the causal attention to bidirectional attention between documents and utilizes model attention values to decide the relative orders of documents instead of using the order provided in input prompts, therefore enabling Position-INvariant inferencE (PINE) at the document level. By eliminating position bias, models achieve better performance and reliability in downstream tasks, including LM-as-a-judge, retrieval-augmented QA, molecule generation, and math reasoning. Notably, PINE is especially useful when adapting LMs for evaluating reasoning pairs: it consistently provides 8 to 10 percentage points performance gains, making Llama-3-70B-Instruct perform even better than GPT-4-0125-preview and GPT-4o-2024-08-06 on the RewardBench reasoning set.

papers.title: On the Pitfalls of Analyzing Individual Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the pitfalls in the common methodology for ranking individual neurons in language models, and how can we better evaluate neuron rankings by separating probe quality from ranking quality and focusing on information used by the model?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies two pitfalls in neuron ranking methods (conflating probe and ranking quality, and focusing on encoded rather than used information), and introduces a probe-less ranking method (PROBELESS) that better identifies neurons actually used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the importance of separating probe quality from ranking quality and of evaluating rankings based on information used by the model, introducing a probe-less ranking method that is effective for identifying causally relevant neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Probe quality and ranking quality are confounded; a good probe can yield high accuracy even with a bad ranking, masking the ranking's true quality.
Encoded information is not the same as information used by the model; a ranking good for probing may not select neurons that are causally important for the model's output.
The proposed PROBELESS ranking, based on simple data statistics, tends to select neurons that are more used by the model than rankings from probe-based methods (LINEAR and GAUSSIAN).
The GAUSSIAN probe often achieves high accuracy by memorizing word-type–label pairs, leading to low selectivity, whereas LINEAR is more stable and selective.
There is an overlap between encoded and used information, but they are not identical, highlighting the need to evaluate rankings based on used information via interventions.
papers.abstract: While many studies have shown that linguistic information is encoded in hidden word representations, few have studied individual neurons, to show how and in which neurons it is encoded. Among these, the common approach is to use an external probe to rank neurons according to their relevance to some linguistic attribute, and to evaluate the obtained ranking using the same probe that produced it. We show two pitfalls in this methodology: 1. It confounds distinct factors: probe quality and ranking quality. We separate them and draw conclusions on each. 2. It focuses on encoded information, rather than information that is used by the model. We show that these are not the same. We compare two recent ranking methods and a simple one we introduce, and evaluate them with regard to both of these aspects.

papers.title: Query-Focused Retrieval Heads Improve Long-Context Reasoning and Re-ranking
papers.research_question: How can we identify a more effective set of attention heads for retrieval in long-context language models, and how can we use them to improve long-context reasoning and re-ranking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces QRHEAD, a set of attention heads identified using query-context attention on realistic data, and QRRETRIEVER, a retriever built on these heads, which improves long-context reasoning and re-ranking performance.
papers.conclusion: QRHEAD are a practical and effective set of attention heads for retrieval, and QRRETRIEVER built on them achieves strong performance on various tasks, offering insights for improving retrieval with LMs.
papers.key_findings:
QRHEAD are more effective than original retrieval heads and full attention heads for retrieval.
QRRETRIEVER improves performance on long-context reasoning tasks (LongMemEval and CLIPPER) by over 10% compared to full context and outperforms dense retrievers.
QRRETRIEVER achieves strong zero-shot re-ranking performance on BEIR, outperforming other LLM-based re-rankers.
QRHEAD generalize across tasks and context lengths.
Both the query-context attention scoring and task selection (realistic data) are crucial for identifying effective heads.
papers.limitation:
Do not explore parameter-updating techniques.
Lack a complete understanding of the internal mechanism of QRHEAD.
Evaluation is limited to passage re-ranking and long-context multi-hop reasoning; unclear if it generalizes to other long-context tasks (e.g., summarization).
Experiments are limited to English datasets.
future_direction: Investigating parameter-updating techniques that leverage insights from QRHEAD.
Applying circuit analysis techniques to dissect the fine-grained behaviors of QRHEAD.
Generalizing to broader long-context tasks and cross-lingual robustness.
papers.abstract: Recent work has identified retrieval heads, a subset of attention heads responsible for retrieving salient information in long-context language models (LMs), as measured by their copy-paste behavior in Needlein-a-Haystack tasks. In this paper, we introduce QRHead (Query-Focused Retrieval Head), an improved set of attention heads that enhance retrieval from long context. We identify QRHead by aggregating attention scores with respect to the input query, using a handful of examples from real-world tasks (e.g., long-context QA). We further introduce QRRetriever, an efficient and effective retriever that uses the accumulated attention mass of QRHead as retrieval scores. We use QRRetriever for long-context reasoning by selecting the most relevant parts with the highest retrieval scores. On multi-hop reasoning tasks LongMemEval and CLIPPER, this yields over 10% performance gains over full context and outperforms strong dense retrievers. We also evaluate QRRetriever as a re-ranker on the BEIR benchmark and find that it achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming other LLM-based re-rankers such as RankGPT. Further analysis shows that both the query-context attention scoring and task selection are crucial for identifying QRHead with strong downstream utility. Overall, our work contributes a general-purpose retriever and offers interpretability insights into the long-context capabilities of LMs.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Decoupling Positional and Symbolic Attention Behavior in Transformers
papers.research_question: What are the mathematical properties underlying positional and symbolic attention behaviors? How can we measure them? How do they relate to RoPE frequencies? How does model performance depend on frequency choices?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical and empirical framework to decouple positional and symbolic attention behaviors in Transformers with RoPE. It introduces a metric to quantify these behaviors and shows how they relate to frequency use, demonstrating that model performance on positional vs. symbolic tasks can be controlled by frequency access.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a detailed understanding of RoPE and how its properties relate to model behavior, decoupling positional and symbolic attention mechanisms and showing they are in tension, with model accuracy depending on the ability to employ appropriate frequencies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in RoPE-based Transformers exhibit a strong correspondence between behavior and frequency use: lower frequencies are used for symbolic behavior, higher frequencies for positional behavior.
Positional and symbolic behaviors are mutually exclusive (positional-symbolic exclusion principle).
The paper introduces a metric to quantify positional and symbolic scores, enabling visualization of the positional-symbolic profile of a model.
Model performance on canonical tasks (index and information retrieval) depends on the frequencies available: positional tasks require higher frequencies, symbolic tasks require lower frequencies.
Controlling which frequencies attention heads can access allows control over model performance on these tasks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a wider set of tasks and models
Investigate whether positional and symbolic behaviors are fundamental building blocks of attention heads
papers.abstract: An important aspect subtending language understanding and production is the ability to independently encode positional and symbolic information of the words within a sentence. In Transformers, positional information is typically encoded using Positional Encodings (PEs). One such popular PE, namely Rotary PE (RoPE), has been widely used due to its empirical success. Recently, it has been argued that part of RoPE's success emerges from its ability to encode robust positional and semantic information using large and small frequencies, respectively. In this work, we perform a deeper dive into the positional versus symbolic dichotomy of attention heads behavior, both at the theoretical and empirical level. We provide general definitions of what it means for a head to behave positionally or symbolically, prove that these are two mutually exclusive behaviors and develop a metric to quantify them. We apply our framework to analyze Transformer-based LLMs using RoPE and find that all heads exhibit a strong correspondence between behavior and frequency use. Finally, we introduce canonical tasks designed to be either purely positional or symbolic, and demonstrate that the Transformer performance causally relates to the ability of attention heads to leverage the appropriate frequencies. In particular, we show that we can control the Transformer performance by controlling which frequencies the attention heads can access. Altogether, our work provides a detailed understanding of RoPE, and how its properties relate to model behavior.

papers.title: Modular Arithmetic: Language Models Solve Math Digit by Digit
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms do LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, specifically focusing on whether they employ digit-position-specific circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates digit-position-specific arithmetic circuits in LLMs, showing that LLMs solve arithmetic tasks digit by digit using modular circuits that causally control individual output digits.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform simple arithmetic using modular, digit-position-specific circuits that operate independently, indicating a structured and compositional approach to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs use distinct, digit-position-specific circuits for units, tens, and hundreds digits in addition and subtraction.
These circuits are causally involved, as targeted interventions selectively alter only the corresponding digit in the output.
The circuits exist across various model sizes and tokenization strategies, including both multi-digit and single-digit tokenization.
Addition and subtraction circuits rely on largely distinct sets of neurons.
Carry operations are handled separately from the digit-position circuits, suggesting additional mechanisms for carry propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to addition and subtraction, not addressing more complex operations like multiplication or division.
Focuses on MLP layers and does not account for the role of attention heads or other residual stream components.
Uses Fisher Score for neuron identification, which may not be the most precise method compared to gradient-based attribution.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Analyzing circuits responsible for composing digit-level results into final outputs.
Using more precise methods like gradient-based attribution for circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: While recent work has begun to uncover the internal strategies that Large Language Models (LLMs) employ for simple arithmetic tasks, a unified understanding of their underlying mechanisms is still lacking. We extend recent findings showing that LLMs represent numbers in a digit-wise manner and present evidence for the existence of digit-position-specific circuits that LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, i.e. modular subgroups of MLP neurons that operate independently on different digit positions (units, tens, hundreds). Notably, such circuits exist independently of model size and of tokenization strategy, i.e. both for models that encode longer numbers digit-by-digit and as one token. Using Feature Importance and Causal Interventions, we identify and validate the digit-position-specific circuits, revealing a compositional and interpretable structure underlying the solving of arithmetic problems in LLMs. Our interventions selectively alter the model's prediction at targeted digit positions, demonstrating the causal role of digit-position circuits in solving arithmetic tasks.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Characterizing Verbatim Short-Term Memory in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of information about the prior context can language models retrieve? Specifically, can they retrieve the exact words (verbatim) that occurred previously in a text?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers implement a working memory-like system that can flexibly retrieve individual token representations verbatim, while LSTMs maintain a coarser, rapidly-decaying semantic gist of prior context.
papers.conclusion: The introduced paradigm can illuminate the memory systems in neural language models, revealing that transformers develop detailed verbatim short-term memory while LSTMs maintain a coarse gist.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers retrieve both the identity and ordering of nouns from prior context, and this retrieval is robust to set size and intervening text length.
Transformer retrieval is learned and depends on attention mechanisms; shuffling attention weights reduces retrieval.
Transformer retrieval improves with larger training corpus and greater model depth.
LSTMs exhibit less precise retrieval, limited to list-initial tokens and short intervening texts, and are not sensitive to word order.
LSTM retrieval improves when the list is semantically coherent.
future_direction: Apply the paradigm to other transformer models (e.g., BERT, T5).
Test LSTM architectures augmented with attention or a copy-mechanism.
Perform targeted ablations of specific attention heads to pinpoint the mechanistic locus of short-term memory.
papers.abstract: When a language model is trained to predict natural language sequences, its prediction at each moment depends on a representation of prior context. What kind of information about the prior context can language models retrieve? We tested whether language models could retrieve the exact words that occurred previously in a text. In our paradigm, language models (transformers and an LSTM) processed English text in which a list of nouns occurred twice. We operationalized retrieval as the reduction in surprisal from the first to the second list. We found that the transformers retrieved both the identity and ordering of nouns from the first list. Further, the transformers' retrieval was markedly enhanced when they were trained on a larger corpus and with greater model depth. Lastly, their ability to index prior tokens was dependent on learned attention patterns. In contrast, the LSTM exhibited less precise retrieval, which was limited to list-initial tokens and to short intervening texts. The LSTM's retrieval was not sensitive to the order of nouns and it improved when the list was semantically coherent. We conclude that transformers implemented something akin to a working memory system that could flexibly retrieve individual token representations across arbitrary delays; conversely, the LSTM maintained a coarser and more rapidly-decaying semantic gist of prior tokens, weighted toward the earliest items.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: The Locality and Symmetry of Positional Encodings
papers.research_question: What are the core properties of positional encodings in BERT-style models, and how do they affect downstream task performance and sensitivity to word order changes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies locality and symmetry as core properties of positional encodings in BERT-style models, shows they correlate with downstream task performance, and reveals a weakness of symmetry via new word-swap probing tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that locality and symmetry are key properties of positional encodings, and that symmetry has a flaw leading to insensitivity to semantic role swaps, which should inspire better design of positional encodings.
papers.key_findings:
Positional encodings in BERT-style models exhibit locality and symmetry, and these properties are learned during pre-training.
Locality and symmetry provide better inductive bias; models initialized with encodings having suitable locality and symmetry achieve better downstream performance.
Locality helps positional encodings capture short-distance syntactic dependencies, while contextual weights capture long-distance dependencies.
Symmetry leads to insensitivity to semantic role swaps, making models fragile to global word order changes that alter sentence meaning.
Existing positional encodings are robust to local word swaps (within constituents) but extremely fragile to global swaps (semantic role swaps).
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on bidirectional masked language models and does not include decoder-only models like GPT.
The analysis is limited to English language; different languages have different word order properties.
The handcrafted positional encodings used replicate the limitations of current encodings and do not solve the symmetry flaw.
future_direction: Extend analysis to decoder-only language models (GPT-style).
Study positional encodings in other languages with different word orders.
Develop new positional encoding architectures that address the symmetry flaw.
papers.abstract: Positional Encodings (PEs) are used to inject word-order information into transformer-based language models. While they can significantly enhance the quality of sentence representations, their specific contribution to language models is not fully understood, especially given recent findings that various positional encodings are insensitive to word order. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of positional encodings in Bidirectional Masked Language Models (BERT-style) , which complements existing work in three aspects: (1) We uncover the core function of PEs by identifying two common properties, Locality and Symmetry; (2) We show that the two properties are closely correlated with the performances of downstream tasks; (3) We quantify the weakness of current PEs by introducing two new probing tasks, on which current PEs perform poorly. We believe that these results are the basis for developing better PEs for transformer-based language models.

papers.title: On the token distance modeling ability of higher RoPE attention dimension
papers.research_question: How do different dimensions in Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) contribute to modeling token distances and long-range dependencies in attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that higher dimensions in RoPE attention heads correlate with longer token distances and identifies 'Positional Heads' with strong distance-dimension correlation that are crucial for long-text comprehension.
papers.conclusion: Higher dimensions in RoPE are more effective at distinguishing token distances, and Positional Heads with correlated dimension allocation are crucial for integrating information across distances in long-text tasks, providing insights for future research.
papers.key_findings:
In most attention heads, higher-dimensional low-frequency components contribute more to attention scores than lower-dimensional high-frequency components.
Input lengths exceeding the pre-training length cause anomalies in high-dimensional components, and length extrapolation extends the high-dimensional attention allocation for longer token distances.
Attention heads with strong correlation between token distance and dimension allocation, termed 'Positional Heads', are key for modeling text distances.
Ablation of Positional Heads significantly reduces model performance on long-context tasks such as question answering and code completion.
The Spearman correlation coefficient can effectively identify Positional Heads based on their distance-dimension correlation.
papers.limitation:
The dimensional decomposition approach is based on the explicit meaning of dimensions in rotary position embeddings and is not applicable to all types of position encodings.
Computational resource constraints limited validation with longer input sequences and analysis of fine-tuning impacts on these attention heads.
future_direction: Leverage the properties of Positional Heads to address challenging tasks such as long text comprehension.
Conduct more detailed experimental analysis with longer input sequences and fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Length extrapolation algorithms based on Rotary position embedding (RoPE) have shown promising results in extending the context length of language models. However, understanding how position embedding can capture longer-range contextual information remains elusive. Based on the intuition that different dimensions correspond to different frequency of changes in RoPE encoding, we conducted a dimension-level analysis to investigate the correlation between a hidden dimension of an attention head and its contribution to capturing long-distance dependencies. Using our correlation metric, we identified a particular type of attention heads, which we named Positional Heads, from various length-extrapolated models. These heads exhibit a strong focus on long-range information interaction and play a pivotal role in long input processing, as evidence by our ablation. We further demonstrate the correlation between the efficiency of length extrapolation and the extension of the high-dimensional attention allocation of these heads. The identification of Positional Heads provides insights for future research in long-text comprehension.

papers.title: How Do Language Models Understand Tables? A Mechanistic Analysis of Cell Location
papers.research_question: How do language models understand tables, specifically the internal mechanisms for processing linearized two-dimensional structured tables?
papers.core_contribution: The paper delineates table understanding into a three-stage pipeline (Semantic Binding, Coordinate Localization, Information Extraction), shows that models use delimiter counting for coordinates, encode column indices in a linear subspace steerable by vector arithmetic, and reuse the same attention heads for multi-cell location.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a comprehensive explanation of table understanding within Transformer architectures, revealing the internal mechanisms that bridge sequential input and two-dimensional logic.
papers.key_findings:
Table understanding in transformers follows a three-stage pipeline: Semantic Binding (early layers), Coordinate Localization (middle layers), and Information Extraction (late layers).
The model locates target cells by counting delimiters (e.g., '|' and newlines) to resolve row and column indices.
Column indices are encoded in a linear subspace, allowing precise steering of model focus via vector arithmetic in the residual stream.
The same set of attention heads identified for atomic cell location are reused for multi-cell location through parallel semantic binding and multi-threaded coordinate localization.
The model's capacity for table understanding degrades with increasing table dimensions.
papers.limitation: The model's capacity for table understanding degrades with increasing table dimensions.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for table-related tasks, the internal mechanisms enabling them to process linearized two-dimensional structured tables remain opaque. In this work, we investigate the process of table understanding by dissecting the atomic task of cell location. Through activation patching and complementary interpretability techniques, we delineate the table understanding mechanism into a sequential three-stage pipeline: Semantic Binding, Coordinate Localization, and Information Extraction. We demonstrate that models locate the target cell via an ordinal mechanism that counts discrete delimiters to resolve coordinates. Furthermore, column indices are encoded within a linear subspace that allows for precise steering of model focus through vector arithmetic. Finally, we reveal that models generalize to multi-cell location tasks by multiplexing the identical attention heads identified during atomic location. Our findings provide a comprehensive explanation of table understanding within Transformer architectures.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Position Information Emerges in Causal Transformers Without Positional Encodings via Similarity of Nearby Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can positional information be stored in causal transformers without explicit positional encodings? The paper investigates the hypothesis that positional information emerges via the similarity of nearby embeddings (the adjacency pattern).
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and demonstrates that positional information in causal transformers without positional encodings can be stored via an 'adjacency pattern', where nearby token embeddings are more similar to each other than faraway ones.
papers.conclusion: Causal attention in transformers without positional encodings induces an adjacency pattern in embeddings, where nearby tokens are more similar, providing a mechanism for storing and potentially recovering positional information.
papers.key_findings:
The adjacency pattern (higher cosine similarity between nearby embeddings) appears in both randomly initialized and trained causal transformers without positional encodings.
This pattern emerges right after the first causal attention layer, even in randomly initialized models.
The adjacency pattern provides a mechanism for the model to potentially reconstruct token positions without explicit encodings.
The pattern is observed across a variety of synthetic tasks (Addition, Reversal, Indexing, Ordering) that require positional information.
The adjacency pattern is distinct from and can exist alongside the variance-based positional information theory proposed by Chi et al. (2023).
papers.abstract: Transformers with causal attention can solve tasks that require positional information without using positional encodings. In this work, we propose and investigate a new hypothesis about how positional information can be stored without using explicit positional encoding. We observe that nearby embeddings are more similar to each other than faraway embeddings, allowing the transformer to potentially reconstruct the positions of tokens. We show that this pattern can occur in both the trained and the randomly initialized Transformer models with causal attention and no positional encodings over a common range of hyperparameters.

papers.title: DoPE: Denoising Rotary Position Embedding
papers.research_question: How does Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) induce massive activations and attention sinks, and how can these effects be mitigated to improve length extrapolation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DoPE, a training-free denoising scheme for RoPE that uses truncated matrix entropy to identify and suppress noisy attention heads, then reparameterizes their attention maps with an isotropic Gaussian distribution, improving length extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: Selective positional encoding via DoPE is key to robust extrapolation, and controlling how positional information is injected across heads is important for long-context robustness.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's low-frequency components concentrate structured energy, producing low-rank, over-aligned attention patterns that manifest as activation noise.
Truncated matrix entropy can identify attention heads dominated by massive activations (attention sinks).
DoPE improves length extrapolation performance without fine-tuning, increases robustness to perturbations, and boosts needle-in-a-haystack and many-shot in-context learning tasks.
Heads with low truncated matrix entropy (denoised heads) often exhibit attention sinks, while high-entropy heads (extrapolative heads) benefit from preserved positional encoding.
Sparse patterns estimated from synthetic tasks (e.g., NIH) transfer to more complex reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH), indicating cross-task generalization.
papers.limitation:
Head selection adds computation, and the entropy-based criteria may not hold across all models, layers, or domains.
Evaluation focuses on long-context inference tasks, so generalization to broader settings remains to be validated.
papers.abstract: Positional encoding is essential for large language models (LLMs) to represent sequence order, yet recent studies show that Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) can induce massive activation. We investigate the source of these instabilities via a spectral analysis of RoPE, and show that its low-frequency components concentrate structured energy, producing low-rank, over-aligned attention patterns. We theoretically reveal that this low-frequency alignment manifests as activation noise, degrading stability during long-context extrapolation. To mitigate this effect, we introduce Denoising Rotary Position Embedding (DoPE), a training-free method that identifies and suppresses noisy attention heads using truncated matrix entropy, then reparameterizes their attention maps with an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Across a range of settings, DoPE improves length extrapolation performance without fine-tuning, increases robustness to perturbations, and boosts both needle-in-a-haystack and many-shot in-context learning tasks. These results suggest that selective positional encoding is key to robust extrapolation. Our project page is Project: https://The-physical-picture-of-LLMs.github.io

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: XAI-based cross-ensemble feature ranking methodology for machine learning models
papers.research_question: Does the single kernel SHAP model provide reliable feature importance rankings for machine learning models, and can an ensemble methodology produce more stable and reliable rankings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an ensemble XAI methodology that combines model performance and SHAP values to calculate a stable and reliable feature importance ranking for both classification and regression models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-ensemble feature ranking methodology solves the unstable factor importance ranking problem of single kernel SHAP and provides stable, reliable rankings for both classification and regression models, paving the way for trustable AI.
papers.key_findings:
Single kernel SHAP produces inconsistent feature importance rankings across different machine learning models for the same dataset.
The proposed cross-ensemble methodology stabilizes the feature importance ranking across models.
The ensemble ranking results are more consistent with human knowledge compared to single-model SHAP or XGBoost feature importance.
The method identified novel potential risk factors for diabetes from non-objective-oriented census data, such as room space and mental situation.
The methodology provides a way to build more trustable AI models through explainability.
papers.limitation:
Only SHAP is used to combine factor contributions; other explanation methods could be explored.
The study only addresses factor importance ranking, not the explanation of factor correlations.
future_direction: Use more reliable explanation methods in addition to SHAP.
Explore how to explain the factors' correlation efficiently.
Build knowledge-based small AI models using the identified factors.
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one robust technology has been used in various fields, making innovative society possible and changing our lifestyles. However, the black box problem is still one big problem for artificial intelligence. In this study, we first compared the results of kernel Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for various machine learning models and found that the single SHAP model cannot explain the models at the human knowledge level. Then the factors’ global ranking was calculated using our proposed ensemble methodology. Finally, the new factors’ ranking was compared with other factor ranking method. Our experimental results declare that the proposed cross-ensemble feature ranking methodology provides stable and comparatively reliable feature ranking in both the classification and regression models.

papers.title: Mitigate Position Bias in Large Language Models via Scaling a Single Dimension
papers.research_question: How can position bias ('lost in the middle') in long-context language models be mitigated by identifying and scaling positional information present in specific hidden state channels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that positional information in hidden states (introduced by the causal mask) is a cause of position bias and introduces a method to mitigate this bias by identifying and scaling a single 'positional channel' in the hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Scaling positional hidden states is an effective and generalizable method for mitigating position bias in LLMs, requiring modification of only one channel and causing minimal side effects on the model's original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weight patterns in retrieval-related layers exhibit a U-shape that correlates with the 'lost in the middle' performance bias.
Positional information from the causal mask is stored in hidden states and affects position bias, independent of position embeddings.
Specific channels (positional channels) in the hidden states exhibit monotonic activation patterns with token position.
Scaling a single identified positional channel in the hidden states, specifically for the last token's attention computation, can significantly mitigate position bias.
The proposed method improves performance on long-context tasks (e.g., up to 15.2% on a 'lost in the middle' benchmark) with minimal impact on general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is applied only to the attention queried by the last token and to a selected range of middle layers, based on engineering experience.
The search algorithm for the optimal channel relies on heuristics (monotonicity, smoothness) and a small calibration dataset.
future_direction: Extend the scaling method to affect the attention of more tokens, not just the last token.
Automate the selection of the scaling factor and the range of layers to apply the scaling.
Explore the integration of the method with other position bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in various real-world scenarios due to their excellent generalization capabilities and robust generative abilities. However, they exhibit position bias, also known as "lost in the middle", a phenomenon that is especially pronounced in long-context scenarios, which indicates the placement of the key information in different positions of a prompt can significantly affect accuracy. This paper first explores the micro-level manifestations of position bias, concluding that attention weights are a micro-level expression of position bias. It further identifies that, in addition to position embeddings, causal attention mask also contributes to position bias by creating position-specific hidden states. Based on these insights, we propose a method to mitigate position bias by scaling this positional hidden states. Experiments on the NaturalQuestions Multi-document QA, KV retrieval, LongBench and timeline reorder tasks, using various models including RoPE models, context windowextended models, and Alibi models, demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach. Our method can improve performance by up to 15.2% by modifying just one dimension of hidden states. Our code is available at https://aka.ms/PositionalHidden.

papers.title: Round and Round We Go! What makes Rotary Positional Encodings useful?
papers.research_question: What makes Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE) useful, and how are they used mechanistically in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that Gemma uses RoPE's high frequencies for robust positional attention patterns and low frequencies for semantic information, and proposes p-RoPE, a modification that truncates low frequencies to improve performance.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a nuanced understanding of RoPE in LLMs, which is crucial for scaling to large context lengths, and the proposed p-RoPE modification shows promise for performance gains.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE does not necessarily decay attention with distance; this decay only occurs under specific conditions (e.g., constant queries and keys).
Gemma 7B prefers to use the low frequencies of RoPE for semantic information, while high frequencies are used for positional attention patterns.
High frequencies enable the construction of robust positional attention heads (e.g., diagonal and previous-token heads).
Low frequencies act as semantic channels but are not robust over long contexts due to rotation.
Truncating the lowest frequencies (p-RoPE) can improve performance and robustness in language modeling.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretations may not cover the entire spectrum of how LLMs use RoPE.
The evaluation of p-RoPE is limited to 2B parameter models and perplexity, which may not reflect downstream performance.
future_direction: More careful evaluation of p-RoPE on larger models and downstream tasks.
Analyzing other positional encodings (e.g., Alibi) in a similar mechanistic way.
Testing the effect of randomized positional encodings on frequency usage.
papers.abstract: Positional Encodings (PEs) are a critical component of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), providing the attention mechanism with important sequence-position information. One of the most popular types of encoding used today in LLMs are Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE), that rotate the queries and keys based on their relative distance. A common belief is that RoPE is useful because it helps to decay token dependency as relative distance increases. In this work, we argue that this is unlikely to be the core reason. We study the internals of a trained Gemma 7B model to understand how RoPE is being used at a mechanical level. We find that Gemma learns to use RoPE to construct robust "positional" attention patterns by exploiting the highest frequencies. We also find that, in general, Gemma greatly prefers to use the lowest frequencies of RoPE, which we suspect are used to carry semantic information. We mathematically prove interesting behaviours of RoPE and conduct experiments to verify our findings, proposing a modification of RoPE that fixes some highlighted issues and improves performance. We believe that this work represents an interesting step in better understanding PEs in LLMs, which we believe holds crucial value for scaling LLMs to large sizes and context lengths.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: The Case for Translation-Invariant Self-Attention in Transformer-Based\n Language Models
papers.research_question: How are positional information encoded in transformer-based language models, and can translation-invariant self-attention be an effective alternative to conventional position embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), a new positional encoding method that satisfies six design criteria and improves performance on GLUE tasks with very few added parameters.
papers.conclusion: Translation invariance emerges in state-of-the-art language models, and TISA is a positional encoding method that satisfies all six design criteria and improves downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Position embeddings in transformer-based language models become increasingly translation-invariant during training, and this invariance correlates with model performance.
Adding TISA to ALBERT improves performance on GLUE tasks with minimal parameter increase.
TISA can be used with or without conventional position embeddings, though performance is better when combined.
papers.limitation:
Lack of computational resources to pretrain TISA-only models from scratch
TISA alone (without position embeddings) does not perform as well as when combined with position embeddings
future_direction: Applying TISA to transformer models in other domains like speech, motion synthesis, and computer vision
Exploring two-stage training with TISA, pre-training on short sequences and then scaling to longer ones
papers.abstract:
